【23】Given the enormous numbers of pyrogenic stimulators， the diagnostic approach is a search for the above-listed cat-egories. The approach is a broad-based evaluation look-ing for any clue that may suggest the underlying cause. It is highly unusual to have fever as the only indicator of a disease or disorder. Localizing fndings by organ or sys-tem is usually revealing. See the applicable chapters of this text based on these accompanying signs or symptoms.

【24】General indicators of a viral infection in an adult are a low-grade fever and associated general aches and pains， a headache， malaise， or fatigue. An adult with a bacterial infection presents with a fever above 103°F and the gen-eral symptoms of a viral infection plus some localizingfindings in the throat， abdomen， or chest. Children， on HnOngs1 the other hand， may run high temperatures with almost any illness， including viral infections， otitis media， measles， and roseola. Very high readings (>105°F) are medical emergencies suggesting intracranial hetnorrhage or tu-mor， pancreatitis， or a bad urinary tract infection. If the temperature remains at this elevation， significant brain damage or malignant cardiac arrhythinias may occur.

【25】When the fever is not obviously tied to a flu or upper respiratory infection， a potential valuable avenue ot ques-tioning is recent travel within or outside the United States.8 Certain fungal infections are endemic to specific regions of the United States. Following the same line of questioning， contact with certain animals such as birds， dogs， cats， rats or other rodents， or livestock suggests a spe-cific infectious organism.

【26】In the past， it was recommended to determine a time curve for fever presentation in an attenipt to attach a spe-cific diagnosis to a specific pattern of fever activity. This approach is now not considered useful as a match-type ap-proach. The temporal sequence， however， may provide valuable clues to the underlying cause.

【27】**MANAGEMENT**

There are two overlapping goals of management：(1) con-trol for excessive fever and ensure adequate hydration and (2) treat the underlying cause if it poses a health risk ISTA1to the patient. Control of fever is rarely necessary unless it reaches the range of 103° to 104°F At this level of fever it may be necessary to use cold packs， alcohol or cold sponges， or cold baths. Generally， this level of fever is well tolerated. If medication is used it is important to give aspirin or acetaminophen every 4 hours without a|删除0换行|break in routine. Giving it only at night may cause a re-actionary occurrence of chills or sweats. It is important not to give aspirin to children， especially those with flu or chicken pox， because of the risk of Reye's syndrome(leads to brain and liver darage or death).

【39】**Sleep and Related Complaints**

【40】**CONTEXT**

【41】If asked， most patients in their life would have a com-plaint of disrupted sleep at some times. Often they can re-late this to a specific event such as a stressful incident， alcohol ingestion， or pain. When it is a prolonged or chronic problem， the patient becomes concerned. The conscious effort to initiate sleep often may worsen the condition. It is interesting to note that underreporting is the standard for one of the most common sleep disor-ders： insomnia. A 1991 Gallup survey found that only5% ofinsomniacs consulted a physician. Approximately30% had mentioned it when presenting to a doctor for other complaints.

【42】It is not always obvious what a person does or does not do during sleep. This is important when considering that the result of sleep dysfunction is excessive sleepiness often without a complaint of disrupted sleep. Instead the primary complaint is tiredness or fatigue. With exces-sive tiredness or fatigue， there is the obvious disruption of functional ability with daily activities； however， the larger concern is the potential danger when driving a car or operating other potentially dangerous machinery.

【43】Although many sleep problems arc transient and/or benign， when a primary sleep disorder is detected， fur-ther evaluation at a sleep laboratory is necessary to identify clearly the cause and plan for subsequent management.

【44】**GENERAL STRATEGY**

【45】**History and Evaluation**

Determine whether the patient is able to describe the complaint， attempting to clarify whether the difficulty is falling asleep， constant interruption of|删除0换行|sleep， inability to fall back to sleep after carry morn-ing awakening，“light”sleep， or other difficulty.

【47】Determine associated problems such as excessive daytime sleepiness.

【48】门Determine possible causes or contributing factors， including the following：

【49】1\. diet related-alcohol， caffcine， food allergy

【50】2\. smoking (more than one pack per day)

【51】3\. drugs-cocaine， over-the-counter (OTC)stin-ulants such as nasal sprays， abuse ofOTC sleep medications， prescription drugs

【52】4\. underlying disorders such as asthma，hypo-or hyperthyroidism， chronic obstructive pul-monary disease， congestive heart failure

【53】5\. painful conditions (headaches； hip，knee，shoul-der，low back，and/or neck pain)

【54】6\. restless legs or muscle cramps

【55】7\. amount of sleep， jet lag， work habits

【56】8\. stress and possible depression

【57】9\. moderate exercise prior to sleep

【58】10\. past diagnosis or treatment of a psychologic/psychiatric disorder

【59】If the patient is presenting with a complaint of fa-tigue or tiredness， it may be necessary to obtain an eyewitness account of his or her sleep pattern.

【60】**Management**

【61】If a primary sleep disorder is suspected， referral to a sleep laboratory is warranted.

【62】NMake recommendations regarding seep hygiene.

【63】(Conservative management may be appropriate when sleep hygiene is the primary cause； however， specific sleep disorders should be referred to a spe-cialist for management.

【64】**RELEVANT ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY**

【65】Sleep is a complex interactive function coordinated by many parts of the brain. The structures that facilitate sleep include the basal forebrain， the dorsal raphe nu-clei， the midline thalamus， and the area around the soli-tary tract in the medulla. Waking is facilitated by the reticular activating system (pons and midbrain) and the posterior hypothalamus. This interaction is dependent on changing levels of serotonin， catecholamines， acetyl-choline， and a host of other neurotransmitters. During sleep there are also fluctuations of hormonal levels that may play a role in the quality of sleep and wakefulness. One example is the decrease in epinephrine and cortisol cou-pled with elevated histamine and other mediator levels be-tween midnightand 4AM. These changes correlate with worsening of asthma at night.

【66】Sleep is generally divided into two phases in relation-ship to changing eye movement and other electrophysi-ologic events： rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. These two dis-tinct states cycle throughout the night at about 90-minute intervals. They are not equal， however. NREM accounts for approximately 80% of total sleep.

【67】NREM sleep is divided into four stages. Stages 3 and4 are referred to as delta sleep. NREM is characterized by slowing of the electroencephalogram (EEG)， with ac-companying muscle relaxation， and slow， rolling eye movements. EEG activity slows dramatically during stages 3 and 4. This dleep sleep occurs mainly in the first few hours of sleeping. During this delta sleep， dreaming is less vivid than it is during REM. Patients awakened during delta sleep recall more thought fragments than actual drearns. Only 5% of patients recall vivid dreams.-

【68】REM sleep is more analogous to wakefulness in that there is a faster EEG rate combined with an increase and variability of autonomic nervous system function. Heart rate， respiration， blood pressure， and penile erec-tions vary widely throughout REM sleep. Peripheral voluntary muscles， however， are paralyzed with the ex-ception of the eyelids. This accounts for the phenome-non of sleep paralysis wherein， upon wakening， an individual is temporarily not able to move. When per-sistent and recurrent， narcolepsy， a disorder of REM sleep， is suggested.

【69】NREM begins first， cycling through its four stages. This is followed approximately 80 to 120 minutes later with the first REM sleep， lasting only about 5 to 10 min-utes. As the night progresses， the intensity and duration of REM sleep increase to about 15 to 45 minutes. Vivid dreaming is a characteristic event of REM sleep. Given that REM sleep becomes more intense and lasts longer as the night progresses， the majority of dreaming occurs in the last few hours ofsleeping.

【70】There is a maturation phenomenon associated with time spent in REM or NREM. Newborns spend 50% of their time in REM and enter REM soon after sleep ini-tiation. The time spent in REM decreases as the newborn matures to as little as 20% by 6 months of age. The cor-responding switch to an adult pattern of REM/N

【39】**Sleep and Related Complaints**

【40】**CONTEXT**

【41】If asked， most patients in their life would have a com-plaint of disrupted sleep at some times. Often they can re-late this to a specific event such as a stressful incident， alcohol ingestion， or pain. When it is a prolonged or chronic problem， the patient becomes concerned. The conscious effort to initiate sleep often may worsen the condition. It is interesting to note that underreporting is the standard for one of the most common sleep disor-ders： insomnia. A 1991 Gallup survey found that only5% ofinsomniacs consulted a physician. Approximately30% had mentioned it when presenting to a doctor for other complaints.

【42】It is not always obvious what a person does or does not do during sleep. This is important when considering that the result of sleep dysfunction is excessive sleepiness often without a complaint of disrupted sleep. Instead the primary complaint is tiredness or fatigue. With exces-sive tiredness or fatigue， there is the obvious disruption of functional ability with daily activities； however， the larger concern is the potential danger when driving a car or operating other potentially dangerous machinery.

【43】Although many sleep problems arc transient and/or benign， when a primary sleep disorder is detected， fur-ther evaluation at a sleep laboratory is necessary to identify clearly the cause and plan for subsequent management.

【44】**GENERAL STRATEGY**

【45】**History and Evaluation**

Determine whether the patient is able to describe the complaint， attempting to clarify whether the difficulty is falling asleep， constant interruption of|删除0换行|sleep， inability to fall back to sleep after carry morn-ing awakening，“light”sleep， or other difficulty.

【47】Determine associated problems such as excessive daytime sleepiness.

【48】门Determine possible causes or contributing factors， including the following：

【49】1\. diet related-alcohol， caffcine， food allergy

【50】2\. smoking (more than one pack per day)

【56】8\. stress and possible depression

【57】9\. moderate exercise prior to sleep

【58】10\. past diagnosis or treatment of a psychologic/psychiatric disorder

【59】If the patient is presenting with a complaint of fa-tigue or tiredness， it may be necessary to obtain an eyewitness account of his or her sleep pattern.

【61】If a primary sleep disorder is suspected， referral to a sleep laboratory is warranted.

【63】(Conservative management may be appropriate when sleep hygiene is the primary cause； however， specific sleep disorders should be referred to a spe-cialist for management.

【64】**RELEVANT ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY**

【65】Sleep is a complex interactive function coordinated by many parts of the brain. The structures that facilitate sleep include the basal forebrain， the dorsal raphe nu-clei， the midline thalamus， and the area around the soli-tary tract in the medulla. Waking is facilitated by the reticular activating system (pons and midbrain) and the posterior hypothalamus. This interaction is dependent on changing levels of serotonin， catecholamines， acetyl-choline， and a host of other neurotransmitters. During sleep there are also fluctuations of hormonal levels that may play a role in the quality of sleep and wakefulness. One example is the decrease in epinephrine and cortisol cou-pled with elevated histamine and other mediator levels be-tween midnightand 4AM. These changes correlate with worsening of asthma at night.

【66】Sleep is generally divided into two phases in relation-ship to changing eye movement and other electrophysi-ologic events： rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. These two dis-tinct states cycle throughout the night at about 90-minute intervals. They are not equal， however. NREM accounts for approximately 80% of total sleep.

【67】NREM sleep is divided into four stages. Stages 3 and4 are referred to as delta sleep. NREM is characterized by slowing of the electroencephalogram (EEG)， with ac-companying muscle relaxation， and slow， rolling eye movements. EEG activity slows dramatically during stages 3 and 4. This dleep sleep occurs mainly in the first few hours of sleeping. During this delta sleep， dreaming is less vivid than it is during REM. Patients awakened during delta sleep recall more thought fragments than actual drearns. Only 5% of patients recall vivid dreams.-

【68】REM sleep is more analogous to wakefulness in that there is a faster EEG rate combined with an increase and variability of autonomic nervous system function. Heart rate， respiration， blood pressure， and penile erec-tions vary widely throughout REM sleep. Peripheral voluntary muscles， however， are paralyzed with the ex-ception of the eyelids. This accounts for the phenome-non of sleep paralysis wherein， upon wakening， an individual is temporarily not able to move. When per-sistent and recurrent， narcolepsy， a disorder of REM sleep， is suggested.

【69】NREM begins first， cycling through its four stages. This is followed approximately 80 to 120 minutes later with the first REM sleep， lasting only about 5 to 10 min-utes. As the night progresses， the intensity and duration of REM sleep increase to about 15 to 45 minutes. Vivid dreaming is a characteristic event of REM sleep. Given that REM sleep becomes more intense and lasts longer as the night progresses， the majority of dreaming occurs in the last few hours ofsleeping.

【70】There is a maturation phenomenon associated with time spent in REM or NREM. Newborns spend 50% of their time in REM and enter REM soon after sleep ini-tiation. 【162】**·Ceruloplasmin is an acute phase protein. It is a ferroxidase that has an essential role in iron metabolism and contains greater than 95% of the plasma copper.**

【163】**·Because ceruloplasmin accounts for 95% of the serum copper， measurement of this value will also be abnormally low in patients with Wilson disease(usually <20 mg/dl， and a level >35 mg/dl almost excludes the diagnosis).**

**On the contrary， the low level of ceruloplasmin can also be seen in the|删除换行|conditions listed below.**

【165】**·Therefore， the diagnosis of Wilson disease cannot be based solely on the low level of ceruplasmin.**

【166】**· A separate condition， aceruloplasminemia， is an inherited disorder ofiron metabolism caused by the complete lack of ceruloplasmin ferroxidase activity caused by mutations in the ceruloplasmin gene. It is characterized by iron accumulation in the brain as well as visceral organs. Clinically， the disease consists of the triad of adult-onset neurologic disease， retinal degeneration， and diabetes mellitus. The neurological symptoms， which include involuntary movements， ataxia， and dementia， reflect the sites of iron deposition.**

【175】**Copper studies： diagnostic values in Wilson disease**

【176】**·Wilson disease is a rare disorder of copper metabolism that results in an accumulation of copper in the liver and subsequently in other organs， mainly the central nervous system and the kidneys.**

【177】**· The myriad manifestations of Wilson disease， ranging from psychiatric illness to any types of movement disorders， make its diagnosis dependent on a high index of suspicion. For neurologists， the diagnosis of Wilson disease should be entertained in any patients under 40 years of age with any types of movement disorders， psychiatric symptoms with liver disease， or mood disorders with minor elevations of liver enzymes. If treated promptly， neurological complications may be reversible.**

【178】**·The measurement of hepatic copper by liver biopsy is considered as a gold standard， and is the most definitive test available for the diagnosis of Wilson disease. Serum ceruloplasmin is a useful screening test in suspected individuals.**

【4】**TREATMENT OF TARDIVE DYSKINESIA**

【5】The American Psychiatric Association Task Force on TD concluded that there is no consistently effective treatment for TD. If the patient is on anticholiner-gics medications， they need to be discontinued because they tend to make TD worse . Examples of withdrawal dyskinesias and chronic dyskinesia were presented in chapter 13.

【6】Medications that have been used to attempt to deal with the TD condition include clonazepam. This benzodiazepine has been reported to reduce the movements of TD for up to nine months， but tolerance to the benefits of the medication develops.Naltrexone in combination with clonazepam has shown effectiveness in improving TD . Botulinum toxin has been used in the treatment of drug-induced dystonias. The toxin binds presynaptically to the cholinergic motor nerve terminal preventing release of acetylcholine and producing a denervated muscle. Although the prevention of acetylcholine release starts within a few hours， the clinical effect does not occur for one to three days； the innervation is gradually restored. The FDA has ap-proved the use of botulinum toxin for treatment ofstrabismus， blepharospasm， and other facial nerve disorders. It also has been used to treat focal neurolep-tic-induced dystonias that may occur as part of tardive dyskinesia (TD)， such as， laryngeal dystonia and refractory torticollis. For the laryngeal dystonia， the toxin is injected percutaneously through the cricothyroid membrane into the thyroarytenoid muscle bilaterally. The response rate is 80 to 90% and the effects last up to three to four months， and sometimes longer. The toxin has also been effective for the treatment of tardive cervical dystonia .

【7】Although initial studies showed some promise for using vitamin E on TD， subsequent studies have failed to demonstrate that alpha-tocopherol is better than placebo . However， vitamin E could be considered as prophylaxis against TD among patients who do not yet display TD and who are exposed to D2 antagonists. The chiefliability ofvitamin E is the development of prolonged bleeding times in vitamin K-deficient patients . A double-blind， placebo-controlled， crossover study suggests
that melatonin may be effective in the treatment of TD .

【8】Use of Atypical Antipsychotics for the Treatment of TD

【9】Clozapine decreases the symptoms ofsevere TD and tardive dystonia. Risperi-done and olanzapine have demonstrated antidyskinetic activity in double-blind trials. It appears that olanzapine has less TD risk than risperidone.

【10】_Olanzapine_

【11】Researchers at Eli Lilly assert that olanzapine reduces the scores of presumptive TD in adult schizophrenics. Kinon， Basson， Stauffer， et al. (1999) reported on a group of 129 adult patients with presumptive TD. The authors concluded that a retrospective analysis of patients with presumptive TD entering olanzapine clinical trials demonstrated a significant reduction of mean AIMS total scores. The marked and persistent effect for up to 30 weeks suggests that olanzapine may contribute to the improvement of TD through a mechanism other than masking of symptoms by the neuroleptic. To address the possibility ofolanzap-ine masking effect on TD symptoms， a second study was conducted by Kinon， Stauffer， Wang， Thi， and Kollack-Walker (2001).7

【12】The authors concluded that olanzapine seems to ameliorate rather than mask symptoms of TD； this effect is concurrent with improvement in clinical psychotic status. Olanzapine may offer a potential treatment alternative for patients with schizophrenia and preexisting TD. The two cited studies appear to demonstrate olanzapine's positive antidyskinetic effects in adults； these ef-fects were maintained even with a marked decrease of olanzapine dose (up to75%)， without decrement of the medication antipsychotic properties. There is no literature on the use of olanzapine for the treatment of TD in children.

【13】_Risperidone_

【14】**Risperidone also has beneficial effects on tardive dykinesia. Ya Mei Bali， Shun-Cheih Yu， and Chao-Cheng Lin (2003) reported on a double-blind placebo controlled study on patients with severe tardive dyskinesia treated for a 12-week period with either risperidone or placebo.The authors noted that approximately70 to 100% oftardive dyskinesia patients show orofacial movements； 20 to 60%limb and truncal movements； and 10 to 50% both orofacial and limb-truncal movements. The study demonstrated that bucco-lingual movements and cho-reathetoid tardive dyskinesia respond differently to risperidone， supporting the proposition that these are two separate syndromes (pp. 1346-1347).**

【19】Schopick (2005) using the conceptualization of an imbalance between the do-paminergic and cholinergic systems， used rivastigmine with good results， on a 16-year-old white male with a diagnosis of severe TD， probably secondary to high doses of risperidone， 12 mg/day， for the previous six months. The patient exhibited persistent choreiform movements of upper and lower limbs， torso， head (facio/oral/buccal)， and neck. The initial AIMS was 18. Patient had been tapered offrisperidone， and was receiving the following medications： quetiapine50 mg TID； Depakote 1200 mg/day； clonidine 0.075 mg BID +0.05 mg QHS； benztropine 1 mg BID； clonazepam 0.125 mg BID. He was also taking Claritin D BID. Although the rivastigmine was very helpful， there were breakthrough symptoms during the day (rivastigmine half-life is only 1.5 hours) even with a TID schedule. The change to donazepil brought about significant improvement without breakthrough symptoms. Two months after the initiation of donazepil the AIMS score was 0. At 15 months of follow-up there was no evidence of TD. Final medication regime： clozapine 250 mg/day； atomaxetine 80 q AM； Depakote ER 1000 mg q AM， and 750 mg q HS； clonidine 0.1 mg TID， and donazepil 5 mg/day.

【24】**TREATMENT OF COGNITIVE SIDE EFFECTS**

【25】Even schizophrenic patients who have scored average or above average in cognitive scores have a decrement in cognitive performance compared to their scores before the onset of their illness. The patient level of cognitive function-ing might be the most important determinant of real-world outcomes .

【26】Evidence for a positive role on cognitive functioning of atypical antipsy-chotics is accumulating： clozapine appears to improve the domains ofattention and verbal fluency， but has limited impact on verbal learning and memory. Risperidone has demonstrated efficacy in improving perceptual and motor processing， reaction time， executive function， working memory and verbal learning and memory. Olanzapine has overall better results than haloperidol in cognitive functioning. Quetiapine has positive effects on verbal reasoning and fluency， immediate recall， executive function， attention， and verbal memory.

【27】Velligan and Glahn (2004) review a number of medications that may hold promise for the treatment of cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia； these drugs are used as adjunctives. Clinical observations and experiences in the adult field may have implications and applications for the treatment and rehabilitation of chronic and severe psychotic children and adolescents. These medications include：

【28】Guanfacine， an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist， increases spatial working mem-ory and attention when used with SGAs. These effects are consistent with the use of guanfacine in the treatment of ADHD.

【29】**Atomaxetine， a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor， increases dopa-mine and norepinephrine in the frontal cortex. Atomaxetine is currently used for the treatment of ADHD.**

【30】Gantamine， which inhibits acetylcholinesterase and modulates nicotinic neurotransmission， is being used for the cognitive improvement of dementia patients.

【31】Glutamine may enhance hypofunction of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) that appears to be present in schizophrenic patients with cognitive deficits.

【32】Ampakine CX-516 improves attention and memory in patients with schizo-phrenia. Ampakines may also increase neurotrophin levels that induce neuroprotection .

【33】Velligan and Glahn (2004) also review psychosocial interventions， so called， cognitive rehabilitation techniques (CRT)， designed to remediate， compensate for， or bypass cognitive deficits， with the goal of improving broad community outcomes for patients with schizophrenia. These techniques may offer some applications for cognitively compromised psychotic children and adolescents. Velligan and Glahn indicate that although the psychosocial techniques have a great deal ofappeal， their evaluation has yielded mixed results and learned skills do not generalize to improvements in adaptive functioning (pp. 75-76).

---------------------------------------------------

【53】Fixed drug eruption and recurrent herpes simplex (HS) are very different diseases. However, they share one characteristic: they always recur at the same site. Unfortunately, both eventualities occur almost always under the same conditions, i.e. when the child has an infection of the upper respiratory tract that is accompanied by fever.

| Lesion type | Erythema, serum-filled blisters. | Erythema, vesicopustules, crusts. |
| Lesion size | From 1 cm to several decimeters. | 1–2 mm. |
| Sequelae | Dusky violaceous, persistent. | Slight, transient discoloration. |
| Recurrence | It recurs until the cause is identified and removed. | It recurs for many years and is not influenced by drugs. |
| Sites of recurrence | The previous ones, to which other, new sites can be added. | The previous ones or sites nearby the previous ones. |

【65】Epidermal necrolysis is characterized by the coming away of large patches of the epidermis due to the action of exfoliating “toxins” that, by spreading through the blood, widely affect the skin. 【18】**_MANAGEMENT_**

【19】Using only total cholesterol measurements to make man-agement decisions may lead to unwarranted concern or confidence. As discussed above， high-normal levels may be the result of lab error or variation. Approximately 20%of men with confirmed CHD have a cholesterol level be-low 200 mg/dL with an HDLe below 35 mg/dL. It is clear that women with high cholesterol levels， especially those who appear healthy， should not be assumed to be at risk unless confirmed with an associated low HDLc. Men who have a low cholesterol level but either are symp-tomatic for CHD or have significant risk factors should be tested for a low HDLc. In the past， a simple ratio was used between total cholesterol and HDLc， but this may be misleading. For example， two individuals may have a ratio of 5：1. In one individual the total cholesterol is240 mg/dL with an HDLc of 48 mg/dL； the other indi-vidual has a total cholesterol of 150 mg/dL with an HDLo of 30 mg d/L. The second individual. may be at more of a risk than the first based on the low HDLe， especially when other risk factors are added.

【20】Generally， level of risk is known to increase by ap-proximately 3% for each 1% increase in total cholesterol for middle-aged men. Based on the Framingham study， the level of risk is determined by adding point values for each risk factor and using a conversion table to deter-mine the percentage of risk . These simple calculations may be helpful in defining risk for the patient and illustrate how significant each additional risk factor becomes. In practical application， the level of concern for two patients with a cholesterol level of 240 mg/dL is obviously different. If the patient is a middle-aged man with any risk factors， monitoring levels while applying intervention with diet or medication is warranted， whereas a woman with the same cholesterol level and a high HDLc would warrant less concern.

The National Cholesterol Education Program pub-lishes an “at-a-glance” quick reference to the Adult Treatment Panel (ATP) III Guidelines.2 They have cre-ated an evidence-based， sequential， step-by-step approach to the management of patients with hyperlipidemia.More than in the past， lifestyle and dietary approaches are em-phasized as initial management in most patient scenarios|删除0换行|except those with serious risk factors. 【18】**_MANAGEMENT_**

【19】Using only total cholesterol measurements to make man-agement decisions may lead to unwarranted concern or confidence. As discussed above， high-normal levels may be the result of lab error or variation. Approximately 20%of men with confirmed CHD have a cholesterol level be-low 200 mg/dL with an HDLe below 35 mg/dL. It is clear that women with high cholesterol levels， especially those who appear healthy， should not be assumed to be at risk unless confirmed with an associated low HDLc. Men who have a low cholesterol level but either are symp-tomatic for CHD or have significant risk factors should be tested for a low HDLc. In the past， a simple ratio was used between total cholesterol and HDLc， but this may be misleading. For example， two individuals may have a ratio of 5：1. In one individual the total cholesterol is240 mg/dL with an HDLc of 48 mg/dL； the other indi-vidual has a total cholesterol of 150 mg/dL with an HDLo of 30 mg d/L. The second individual. may be at more of a risk than the first based on the low HDLe， especially when other risk factors are added.

【20】Generally， level of risk is known to increase by ap-proximately 3% for each 1% increase in total cholesterol for middle-aged men. Based on the Framingham study， the level of risk is determined by adding point values for each risk factor and using a conversion table to deter-mine the percentage of risk . These simple calculations may be helpful in defining risk for the patient and illustrate how significant each additional risk factor becomes. In practical application， the level of concern for two patients with a cholesterol level of 240 mg/dL is obviously different. If the patient is a middle-aged man with any risk factors， monitoring levels while applying intervention with diet or medication is warranted， whereas a woman with the same cholesterol level and a high HDLc would warrant less concern.

【4】The roentgenographic appearance of malignant lym-phoma can vary widely (159，185a，190，202). Lymphoma tends to involve a large portion of the affected bone and is usually localized in the shaft. The lesion may be marked by a large area of geographic， lytic bone destruction ， may exhibit a moth-eaten pat-tern ， or may have a very subtle permeative pattern involving the medullary canal(165). In the latter case， radiographs may appear almost normal . This lesion may also have an ivory bone appearance， a picture commonly seen in vertebrae or flat bones， although this presentation is not as common as in Hodgkin lymphoma. Although in the past it was thought that lymphoma rarely evokes any periosteal new bone formation and soft tissue mass， in distinct contrast to the presentation of Ewing sarcoma(174)， the recent investigations suggest something dif-ferent. Mulligan et al. (193)， in reviewing 237 pathologi-cally proven cases of primary lymphoma of bone， noted periosteal reaction in 58% and soft tissue masses in 48%of cases. Moreover， Manaster (189) observed a promi-nent endosteal reaction that is rather characteristic for lymphoma. This reaction， together with periosteal re-sponse， caused substantial thickening of the cortex. Fur-thermore， this author suggested that the character of a soft tissue mass may be helpful in the diagnosis of lym-phoma. Whereas the soft tissue mass in most bone sarco-mas is usually round or oval， displacing adjacent muscles and neurovascular bundles， the soft tissue mass in primary lymphoma of bone is often disproportionately large， exhibits an infiltrative appearance involving more than one compartment， extends over long distances， and does not appear to be pseudoencapsulated (189).

【5】The radionuclide bone scan is usually positive(187，197) ， and the combination of a normal radiograph and positive scintigraphy should suggest the possibility of malignant lymphoma (83).

【6】CT can reveal bone destruction and soft tissue involvement， often associated with osseous changes(171，188) . It also can detect bony sequestra， which are estimated to occur in 11% of primary lymphomas of bone (192，193)

【19】**_Histopathology_**

【20】Malignant lymphoma of bone appears grossly similar to lymphomas elsewhere in the body (e.g.， in lymph nodes). Both lesions are soft and fleshy. Areas of necro-sis are occasionally observed (198).

From the histologic standpoint， the appearance of lymphoma is also diverse (191). The lesion consists of ag-gregates of malignant lymphoid cells that fill the marrow spaces and induce resorption of cancellous bone trabec-ulae or reactive sclerosis. In primary non-Hodgkin lym-phoma， diffuse growth pattern is invariably observed， typically exhibiting a mixture of small lymphocytic cells and a larger histiocytic cell component， whereas second-ary lymphomas present with a mixture of paratrabecular， nodular， interstitial， and diffuse infiltration patterns(156). The cells in primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma are usually rounded， ovoid， and pleomorphic . The cytoplasm is basophilic and exhibits well-defined outlines (166) . Unlike the case in Ewing sarcoma， the nuclei are rather large， contain relatively scanty chromatin， and aresometimesindented(cleaved) or horseshoe-shaped， with prominent nucleoli. Cytoplasmic glycogen is usually lacking and reticulin fibers are usually present， forming a more or less uniformly distributed net around the tumor cells(138) . A fibroblastic component is often prominent in intraosseous lymphomas and is sometimes|删除0换行|associated with spindling of the neoplastic lymphoid cells (97). Depending on the type of lymphoma， the in-filtrate may be monomorphic or polymorphic . However， even in the polymorphic variant， the cells are characterized by malignant rather than inflam-matory properties. T-cell lymphomas， in particular， tend to exhibit the widest admixture of cell types， and also tend to be infiltrated by eosinophils (156). The histo-logic differential diagnosis includes Ewing sarcoma/PNET， metastatic neuroblastoma， and other small round cell tumors involving bone. Although the patient’s age and the overall morphologic features are usually suffi-cient to categorize the tumor， the most important single procedure to distinguish lymphoma from all other ma-jor round cell tumors， as already mentioned， is the im-munoreaction for CD45 or CD20  and CD3 (B-cell and T-cell markers) because lymphoid cells are the only cells that show positivity .

【22】When a lymphoma of bone is suspected， all special studies usually done in lymphoma affecting lymph nodes should be performed.

Most cases of Hodgkin lymphoma occur in patients aged 20 to 60 years， with-out an outstanding peak age (127). Secondary bone in-volvement is detected radiologically in 5% to 21% of patients (157，160，176). Primary Hodgkin lymphoma of bone is extremely rare (164，173) and usually involves the spine， humerus， and femur (97，195). Thus far， seven cases of multifocal primary osseous Hodgkin lym-phoma have been described(172).

【32】Symptoms include pain， often with an onset before the lesion becomes visible by radiography. Occasionally a swelling over the affected bone can be noted (163). In the majority of cases with secondary osseous involve-ment， the spine and other bones with abundant red bone marrow， such as ribs， pelvic bones， and femur， are affected. The lesion is frequently sclerotic (e.g.， ivory ver-tebra)  or mixed (lytic with sclerotic patches). A purely lytic geographic pattern is uncommon.

【33】It is difficult to make a specific diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma of bone， largely because the histologic ap-pearance may not be as classic as in cases involving the lymph nodes (183). In the latter， according to the current classification based on biological and clinical data and proposed by the WHO， two entities can be separated： nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkir lymphoma (comprising 5%) and classical Hodgkin lym-phoma (comprising about 95%) with its four subtypes一nodular sclerosis， mixed cellularity， lymphocyte-rich， andlymphocyte-depleted (204). These subtypes differ in their sites， clinical features， and morphologic appear-ance but not in their immunophenotype. The prognos-tic significance of this histologic classification has lost its value with the advent of modern multimodal treatment modalities. Today， the stage and the presence of sys-temic symptoms are much more important (205). It is noteworthy that patients who present with Hodgkin lymphoma in bone almost always have involvement of the lymph nodes， especially the retroperitoneal nodes.

【36】Histologically， Hodgkin lymphoma is distinguished from other lymphomas by the presence of mononu-clear Hodgkin cells and multinuclear Reed-Sternberg cells. The latter are distinctive large cells with sharply delineated abundant cytoplasm and a mirror-image double nucleus rich in chromatin， with a large， promi-nent central eosinophilic nucleolus (161) . These large nucleoli， almost the size of a small lym-phocyte， give the cell a conspicuous and almost specific“owl’s eyes" appearance. Although pathognomonic Reed-Sternberg cells may be difficult to find， the im-munochemical marker CD30 is useful for distinguish-ing them (205) .

【38】**Radiology**

【39】The radiologic differential diagnosis must include other primary bone tumors. If the patient is an infant or a child (up to 10 years of age)， metastatic neuroblastoma should be considered. Between the ages of 5 and 25years， particularly if the lesion is osteolytic or has a moth-eaten or permeative pattern of bone destruction with lamellated or onion-skin periosteal reaction， Ewing sar-coma may be difficult to exclude (127). In more sclerotic lesions， particularly if the “sunburst"pattern of pe-riosteal reaction is present， osteosarcoma is a serious con-sideration. If a sclerotic lesion extends into the articular end of bone， Paget disease should be considered . In patients older than the age of 40 or 50 years， _metastatic carcinoma and plasmacytoma are differential pos-_ sibilities. At any age， osteomyelitis should be a diagnostic consideration. 【46】**Pathology**

【47】The main considerations are similarly appearing Ewing _sarcoma， metastatic neuroblastoma， and metastatic carcinoma._ Rarely， osteomyelitis with abundant lymphocytic cells is a differential possibility. The use of antibodies against CD45 and other lymphocytic antigens will almost invari-ably reveal the lymphoid character of lymphoma tumor cells (127，185).

【48】Most lymphomas exhibit a variety of cytologic features within the lesion， making the histologic appearance that of a polymorphous growth. This is helpful in differentiat-ing malignant lymphoma from Ewing sarcoma， which exhibits a growth of isomorphic small cells. The cells in lymphomas usually are less round than those in Ewing sarcoma， and they tend to have larger regular or even cleaved nuclei .

【49】Another differential diagnostic consideration in a le-sion suspected to be lymphoma of bone is a leukemic infiltrate of bone. However， all patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia have peripheral blood abnor-malities， and if the bones are affected the diagnosis should not be difficult. The same is true of patients with chronic myeloid (granulocytic) leukemia. Chronic and acute myeloic leukemia may present as a primary _bone neoplasm， termed myeloic (granulocytic) sarcoma or_ chloroma. The clinical and radiologic features of this condition may be similar to those oflymphoma. Biopsy specimens will exhibit sheets of large blast-like cells， al-though it is very difficult to make a specific diagnosis of granulocytic sarcoma from routine sections of bone. When this diagnosis is suspected， it is necessary to do immunohistochemical studies such as the reaction for lysozyme and myeloperoxidase， which are considered the most helpful study because the blast cells will be positive. The acid chloracetate-esterase reaction is also helpful. Granulocytic sarcoma， however， may be posi-tive for CD99 similar to Ewing sarcoma and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

【50】The histologic differential diagnosis of malignant lymphoma also includes benign conditions such1 _2S_ II以 chronic osteomyelitis and other types of small cell malignan- _cies such as metastatic carcinoma and Ewing sarcoma._ Chronic osteomyelitis is usually characterized by a mix-ture of inflammatory cells and no evidence of cytologic atypia. There is also a proliferation of capillaries in the background， as well as fibrosis. It may be difficult to distinguish2a large cell lymphoma from metastatic carcinoma or amelanotic melanoma. In these instances. special reactions using CD45， S-100， and cytokeratin antibodies may be helpful in making the distinction. Pos-itivity of the undifferentiated cells for CD45 is strong evi-dence for a malignant lymphoma， whereas positivity for anti-keratin and S-100 protein suggests respectively an epithelial origin of the tumor or melanoma.

【51】Sometimes it is difficult to distinguish a lymphoma from a true sarcoma of bone. Lymphomas of bone may possess spindle cells that occasionally have a storiform pattern， suggesting the diagnosis of malignant fibrous

【52】_histiocytoma. Malignant filrrous histiocytomas usually create_ large areas of bone destruction. If the lesion appears to be only permeative， i.e.， it fills the marrow spaces and leaves behind normal bony trabeculae， the diagnosis of malignant lymphoma with spindling can be suspected. The immunoperoxidase reaction may be helpful in this instance because the spindle cells in malignant lym-phoma react positively with CD45， whereas the spindle cells of malignant fibrous histiocytoma are negative. However， it should be noted that acidic decalcification of bone biopsy specimens may interfere with IHC， because certain antigenic determinants are denatured by brisk acid decalcification.

【53】Occasionally， the eosinophilic component and the histiocytes may be such prominent features of Hodgkin lymphoma as to suggest the diagnosis of LCH (38). In this situation， the age of the patient is crucial： in a middle-aged or elderly patient， the diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma is much more likely and should be strongly considered (182). Additionally， cells in LHC are positive for CDla and S-100 protein， and negative for CD30， whereas Hodgkin lymphoma exhibits the reverse pattern.

source_info.text:
association of epilepsy with psychiatric disorders is as old as medi-cine itself. Epilepsy was considered a psychiatric disorder with a func-tional etiology for most ofrecorded history . Classical neurologists of the late 19th century， such as Hughlings Jackson and W. R. Gowers， were the first to provide a physiological explanation of epilepsy. Countering the prevailing psychiatric opinion of the time， Gowers (1881) found significant persisting mental status abnormalities in only 7% of his series of over 1，000 epileptic patients. The neurologi-cal and psychiatric literature on the relationship between epilepsy and psychopathology have developed separately， for the most part. Much of the literature in this area is anecdotal， and methodological difficulties have been outlined by Hermann and Whitman (1986). Some researchers hypothesize that epilepsy causes psychological changes through direct neural effects while others implicate difficulties adapting to a chronic|删除0换行|illness. Other investigators emphasize antiepileptic medications in the genesis of psychopathology， and some argue that epilepsy and psy-chopathology simply co-occur with no causal relationship between them. A recent， well-controlled study among 241 Icelandic epileptics who were on disability casts doubt on the association of epilepsy and psychopathology . The authors did not find any difference in the prevalence of non-organic psychiatric disorders among disabled epileptic patients of normal intelligence com-pared to disabled patients with other chronic discases. Despite these continuing doubts， a brief review of the literature on interictal mood disorders， anxiety disorders， psychoses， and behavioral and personality disturbances in patients with seizure disorders is presented below.**

【1】**Mood Disorders**

【2】**It remains unciear whether patients with epilepsy are more prone to affective disorders than patients with other medical conditions. There is an increased incidence of mood disorders in patients with neurologic disease similar to that found in chronic medical illnesses that do not affect the brain . In a meta-analysis of 47 studies involving over 2500 patients with epilepsy， other neurological disorders， chronic medical conditions， and controls， Whitman， Hermann， and Gordon (1984) found that although epilep-tics had a higher risk for pathology on the MMPI than did normal con-trois， there was no increase of psychopathology in epilepsy compared with other disorders such as cardiac disease，asthma，arthritis， and renal disease. Moreover， no difference in frequency of psychopathology was found between temporal lobe and generalized epilepsy. Those with mixed reurological disorders had significantly higher risk for abnormal MMPI profiles than epileptics or chronic medical patients.**

【3】**Dodrill and Batzel (1986) found similar results in their meta-analysis of 17 studies using standardized measures including the MMPI. Patierits with epilepsy had more emotional and psychological problems than normals， but there were no significant psychological differences com-pared to patients with other neurological conditions. Also， temporal lobe epileptics did not show more psychological problems than patients with other forms of epilepsy. The number of different seizure types suf fered by the individual patient was a more powerful predictor of psy-chopathology than was any particular seizure type.**

**Mendez， Cummings， and Benson (1986) examined patients with and without epilepsy who also had comorbid major depression and found|删除0换行|few differences between the two. There was no relation between severity of depression and seizure frequency， or between the duration of depres-sion and anticonvulsant dosages or blood levels. However， duration of epilepsy has been correlated with severity of depression， but the type， severity， and specific features of depression are apparently not influ-enced by the age of onset of epilepsy the type of epilepsy， the location of seizure onset， or seizure frequency . Several investigators have found an association between left teiporal lobe epileptic foci and interictal depressive states. In a recent study， 62% of patients with partial complex seizures had a history of interictal depressive disorders， and more patients with left-sided EEG ictal onset had a history of depression . However， more patients had a history of major depressive episodes when there was clear hypometabolism on positron emission tomography regardless of the side of temporal lobe onset. Victoroff， Benson， Grafton， Engel， and Mazziotta (1994) exam-ined 272 epilepsy outpatients whose seizures originated from a structur-al brain lesion other than mesial temporal lobe sclerosis and found that sustained depression had occurred in 25 (9%) cases of symptomatic epilepsy. Depressed patients were compared to those without depres-sion on location of lesion laterality and other seizure history variables， and the only group difference was unilateral left hemisphere lesions in58% of the patients with depression compared with only 21% of the non-depressed patients (x"=10.4，p=0.006). This finding supports the idea of an association between depression and structural lesions in the left hemisphere， but it cannot parcel out the specific contribution of epilepsy to depression. Regardless of the underlying cause of depres-sion in epilepsy， it is important to recall that the coexistence ofepilepsy and depression is fairly common . This should not， however， be interpreted to mean that there is a common underlying neurologic etiology between epilepsy and depression. There is not enough information at this time to determnine whether bipolar disorder or dysthymia is more conon in patients with seizure disorders.**

**With regard to treatment， phenobarbital， vigabatrin， and antiepilep-tic drug polypharmacy reportedly contribute to depressive symptoma-tology . Neuropsychologists should also be aware that antidepressant medications can lower seizure threshold and interact with various anticonvulsant drugs . Furthermore， antiepileptic medications can alter the metabolism of|删除0换行|antidepressant drugs leading to low serum concentrations and a Ion-therapeutic effect . Since treatment with multiple antiepileptic drugs may induce and help maintain depressive states， changing to antiepileptic monotherapy， if possible， may improve the patient's depression . Since monoamine oxidase inhibitors， many tricyclic antidepressants， and some atypical antidepres-sant drugs (e.g.， bupropion) lower seizure threshold， Tucker and McDavid (1997) advocate using selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in patients with comorbid major depression and epilepsy. Detailed reviews of the relationship between epilepsy and depression literature are available .**

【6】**Anxiety Disorders**

【7】**As with other psychiatric disorders， there is no clear and convincing evi-dence that epilepsy causes anxiety disorders through direct physiologi-cal mechanisms. Nevertheless， patients with epilepsy may develop anxiety disorders as a secondary emotional reaction to their chronic ill-ness. Also， patients with partial complex seizures may have symptoms during their seizures that are similar， if not identical， to those of patients with various anxiety disorders . Symptoms that may occur in either partial complex seizures or panic disorder include fear， derealization， misperceptions， itlusions， depersonalization， deja v， jamais vu， dizziness， paresthesias， chills， and hot flashes . The overlapping symptoms of panic disorder and some partial complex seizures suggest that these dis-orders may involve dysfunction of similar brain regions or neural sys-tems. The mesial temporal lobe structures have been implicater in emnotional behavior (i.e.， fear and anxiety) and autonomic responsive-liess (e.g.， heart rate， skin conductance response， blood pressure) and are a frequert location for epileptic foci in partial complex seizure patients . Panic disorder patierts have been found to have abnormal blood flow on PET scans in the area of the hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus， greater in the right hemisphere， as well as abnormally high whole-brain metabolism. Considered together， these investigations implicate the anterior mesial temporal lobe in the genesis of fear and anxiety regardless of etiology. From a clinical perspective， panic disor-ders and partial complex seizures may be distinguished in several ways(Handal， Masand， & Weilburg. 1995； Roth & Harper， 1962； Tucker &**

【8】**McDavid， 1997)： in panic disorders EEGs are normal， consciousness is preserved， olfactory hallucinations are rare， a positive family history of anxiety disorder is common， and symptoms often do not respond to antiepileptic drugs.**

【9】**Tucker and McDavid (1997) describe anxiety symptoms that overlap with partial complex seizures in obsessive-compulsive disorder， post-traumatic stress disorder， and agoraphobia. Patients with complex partial seizures and obsessive-compulsive disorders may both have obsessions， forced thoughts， or intrusive thoughts. Both seizure and anxiety disor-der patients may experience distressing or recurrent recollections， flashback-like episodes， irritability， and concentration difficulties. Finally， patients with epilepsy and agoraphobia both may have fears of recurrent episodes that result in a restriction of their activities. Little is known about the brain mechanisms underlying anxiety. There is anec-dotal evidence of improvement in two cases of obsessive-compulsive dis-order with comorbid epilepsy following treatment with carbamazepine. This led Koopowitz and Berk (1997) to speculate that obsessive compul-sive symptoms may be a variant of epileptiform forced thinking in some patients that may be preferentially responsive to antiepileptic medica-tions. When patients with seizure disorders have comorbid anxiety disorders， cognitive-behavioral intervention and pharmacologic treat-ment using antianxiety medications is common practice. Tucker and McDavid caution that benzodiazepines should be used judiciously with epileptic patients because of concern about tolerance and possible withdrawal seizures.**

【10】**Dissociative Disorders**

**There is a significant overlap in the symnptoms experienced by patients with partial complex seizures and patients with dissociative disorders without comorbid seizures. In a series of 270 patients with partial com-plex seizures of temporal lobe origin， 47% had complex subjective experiences such as derealization (feelings of strangeness or unreality)， depersonalization， feelings of fear， deja vu， and jamnais vu . Similarly parlial complex seizure patients who under-went 24-hour vidco-EEG monitoring for possible epilepsy surgery at the Medical College of Georgia had statistically significantly more frequent and severe subjective symptoms relative to normal controls. These sub~jective symptoms included illusions of peripheral movement， episodic anesthesias， sick headache， speech problems， word finding lapses，|删除0换行|jamais vu， deja vu， memory gaps， unrecalled behaviors， staring spells， mental decline， loss of consciousness， daytime somnolence，and noctur-nal sweating . Many of these self-reported symp-toms are similar to those found in patients with dissociative amnesia(also called psychogenic amnesia)， dissociative fugue， dissociative identity disorder (also known as multiple personality disorder)， and depersonalization.**

【12】**Despite the similarity between the symptoms in dissociative states and partial complex epilepsy， especially of temporal lobe origin， little is known about the possible common underlying mechanisms in the two disorders. In epilepsy， these symptoms are more typically perr-ictal or ictal experiences； this may be useful in differentiating seizures from dis-sociative phenomena. Epileptic symptoms that are similar to dissocia-tive phenomena will typically last for only brief periods of time (seconds or minutes) while dissociative states may last for hours or even days. Also， a history of physical or sexual abuse is less common among epilep- _sy patients. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-fV_  mentions seizure disorders as one of the more common conditions to consider in the differential diagnosis of dissociative disorders. Dissociative amnesia may be differ-entiated from epilepsy by the sudden onset of memory impairment in seizures， and the frequent concomitant motor abnormalities (e.g.， con-vulsions， automatisms) that usually accompany seizures but are usually absent in dissociative amnesia. Also， EEG abnormalities are likely to be encountered in seizure disorders， but not in dissociative amnesia.**

【13】**DSM-IVsuggests similar methods to differentiate between dissociative fuge and epilepsy . Although patients with partial complex seizures may wander or show semipur-poseful behaviors peri-ictally or ictally for which they are subsequently amnesic， patients with dissociative fugue can usually be distinguished from seizure patients on the basis of history and laboratory tests. For example， partial complex seizure patients will usually have an aura， motor abnormalities， stereotyped behaviors， a post-ictal state， and abnormal EEG findings， all of which would be absent in dissociative fugue. Similar techniques would be beneficial in distinguishing partial complex seizures and other dissociative states such as dissociative identi-ty disorder or multiple personality disorder and depersonalization dis-order . The neuropsychologist should also keep in mind that epilepsy and dissociative disorders may co-exist with no causal link whatsoever.**

【14】**Psychoses**

【15】**Although psychotic-like symptoms can occur during a seizure， it remains unclear whether interictal psychoses， such as schizophrenia， are more common among epileptics than in patients with other neuro logical or medical conditions. Unfortunately， this area of investigation is fraught with methodological problems that make it difficult to reach firm conclusions. Although there are a multitude of studies concerned with psychosis in epilepsy， investigations are often not comparable due to differences in patient selection， criteria used for diagnosis of both psychosis and epilepsy， failure to specify seizure type， and frequent lack of EEG classification . As in other psychiatric conditions， it inust be specified whether the symptoms of interest occur ictally， peri-ictally， or during periods with no clinical seizures (interictal-ly). Similar to other psychiatric illnesses， estimates of the frequency of psychosis in epilepsy are highest among psychiatric samples and lowest in nenrological samples. For example， Bash and Mahnig (1984) found evidence of psychosis in 122 of 203 (60%) epileptic inpatients on a psy-chiatric unit while estimates of psychosis among outpatients with epilep-sy in general practice and neurological clinics are considerably lower， ranging from 0%-4%. Nevertheless， even the more conservative estimates of psychosis in epilepsy of approximately 2%-3%  are still slightly higher than the rate of either epilepsy (0.5%-1%) or schizo-phrenia (0.5%-1%) in the general population . Furthermore， in a thorough large-scale community survey of the entire epileptic population of Iceland， 7.1% were current-ly or had at some time been psychotic . Thus， there is probably something inherent in epilepsy or the epilepsy experi-ence that increases the likelihood of psychosis.**

**There are several hypotheses concerning the mechanisms that underlie the association between epilepsy and psychosis. Hypotlheses regarding this association are almost always concerned with partial com-plex seizures of temporal lobe origin. First， the effects of repeated seizures on the brain may lead to changes in limbic and related struc-tures over time that eventually result in a schizophrenic-like psychosis. Support for this idea comes from the notion of“para-doxical”or “forced normalization”where there is an inverse relation~ship between the frequency of partial complex seizures and the presence of psychosis . There is some evidence suggesting that a second epileptic focus may develop|删除0换行|following the repeated spread of seizure activity from a primary focus， possibly through some form of kindling. Kindling has not been docu-mented in humans， however. Moreover， the kindling hypothesis for the development of psychosis in epilepsy has not adequately addressed the neurochemical mechanisms by which the spread of seizures could result in psychosis .**

【17】**Stevens (1986) suggested that recurrent seizures can cause damage to the brain， such as hippocampal cell loss， which in turn may lead to psychosis. In this view it is not the direct effects of the seizures that cause the psychosis， but rather the secondary structural brain damage caused by the seizures that may lead to psychosis in some cases. Others have also emphasized structural brain lesions as the common etiological fac-tor underlying both epilepsy and psychosis so that epilepsy and psy-chosis only co-occur and are only causally related by some third factor， namely a structural lesion . Sachdev (1998) suggested that structural brain abnormalities， such as cortical dysgenesis， may underlie both epilepsy and psychosis， that seizures can modily the presentation of the psychosis， and that psychosis may also alter the presentation of epilepsy. This could complicate the clinical picture of epilepsy with co-morbid psychosis.**

**A third hypothesis suggests that psychosis in epilepsy is a secondary emotional reaction related to psychosocial problems associated with having a chronic medical condition. Schiffer and Babigian (1984) cval-uated patients with multiple sclerosis (MS)， temporal lobe epilepsy(TLE)， and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and found that although MS and TLE patients have more major psychiatric disorders， there were no significant differences between MS and TLE. Standage and Fenton (1975) concluded that chronic diseases carry a non-specific increased risk for psychopathology after they could find no differences in psychological disorders between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and those with peripheral medical disorders， such as arthritis and spondylitis. There are numerous studies that either support or counter each of these hypotheses ， and it remains unknown whether psychosis in epilepsy is due to primary physio-logical， psychological or other factors， or even some combination of these. With regard to clinical practice， Tucker and McDavid (1997) provide|删除0换行|the following diagnostic clues that suggest psychosis may be due to“organic”factors including epilepsy： (1) does not meet DSM-IV criteria for any of the major psychotic disorders， (2) good premorbid social|删除1换行|history， (3) abrupt change in personality， mood， or ability to function，(4) rapid fluctuations in mental status， and (5) unresponsiveness to usual biological or psychological interventions. Perhaps a negative psy-chiatric family history could be added to their list. From a practical standpoint， new onset acute psychosis in patients with known seizure disorders requires thorough inpatient evaluation . A detailed history of both the seizure disorder and the psychosis is necessary. Accurate characterization and diagnosis of the psychotic state is important. The medical workup should be geared toward find-ing treatable or potentially treatable causes such as antiepileptic drug intoxication， chronic subdural hematoma， closed head injury， or neo-plasm. EEG may be of use in identifying encephalopathy， intoxication， or focal status epilepticus. Laboratory evaluation is important in deter-mining possible adverse effects of antiepileptic medications， such as hyponatremia with carbamazepine or hyperammonemia with valproate，**

【19】**In patients with chronic interictal psychoses， pharmacological treat-ment using both antipsychotic and antiepileptic drugs is standard med-ical practice. Medical treatment of psychosis in epilepsy is usually not significantly di
