**Cells can be arrested in metaphase by the administration of a stathmokinetic agent. Early studies on sheep were performed using systemic colcimid to study growth in different seasons. Cells with metaphase nuclei are counted and expressed as a proportion of the whole (metaphase index). Vincristine， which inhibits the production of the mitotic spindle， is probably the best agent； it has been used to examine hair growth in pig skin， but not in human hair. A dose-response curve needs to be calculated prior to its use， and this has only been done for squamous epithelia. The rate of increase of the metaphase index is proportional to the number of cells entering mitosis and therefore to the birth rate of cells in the time between injection and sampling the tissue. The metaphase index，|删除0换行|therefore， differs from the labelling index， which only gives a static measurement with no information concerning cell production. The metaphase arrest technique provides a measure of the rate of cell production. It is a more accurate and enlightening method and should be used to study hair follicles.**

【5】**Neuropsychologists understand the importance of methodologically sound instruments. Clinical assessmnents and research studies can only be as good as the measurement tools they emnploy and the training of those who administer those ineasures. We are now facing a crucial choice as we apply our scientific methods to the study of neuropsycholo-gy in non-English-speaking populations. Errors of language usage must be eliminated from our measures if we are to anticipate any progress in this scientific endeavor. If we do not value this work enough to hold it up to the accepted standards in the field， we are wasting our time and effort. At best， such work will be unusable and rapidly forgotten. At worst， it. will damage our credibility among our international colleagues and insult the very populations we seek to serve.**

**An examination of the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct  reveals a num-ber of standards that can guide the concerned neuropsychologist on this issue. Existing standards are used to make recommendations on how to proceed in the event of non-English-speaking referrals. First，“Psychologists accord appropriate respect to the fundamental rights， dignity， and worth of all people”(Principle D). Furthermore， they “are aware of cultural， individual， and role differences， including those due|删除0换行|to age"(Principle D)， and “they do not engage in unfair discrimination based on age， gender， race， ethnicity， national origin， religion， sexual orientation， language， and socioeconomic status， or any basis pro-scribed by law" (1.10). Some cogently argue that the APA ethics code falls short in areas relevant to culturally sensitive practice . Some go further and ask for a revision of the psychology curriculum to respond to a changing United States population. Christine Iijima Hall (1997) calls the growing obsolescence of psychology “cultural malpractice.”**

【7】**Assess Linguistic Competence**

【8】**In the clinical context， psychologists are obligated to provide only those services that fall “within the boundaries of their competence， based on their education， training， supervised experience， or appropriate profes-sional experience" (1.04a). As mentioned earlier， with regard to level of fluency， competence cannot be assumed but must first be verified. A simple rule of thumb would be to ask oneself，“Could I enroll in a for-eign university's graduate or professional program and successfully engage in all academic activities (reading， writing， speaking， listening， and thinking at an advanced level)?" If the answer is no， the clinician should either seek the necessary language training in order to obtain that level， or simply decline to work with this particular linguistic group. The vast majority of those who possess this level of fluency have com-pleted advanced studies in the target language. This does not mean majoring in French in a domestic university or spending a semester in Mexico. Individuals with this level of fluency usually have lived and stud-ied in the country of the target language for some years. Some clini-cians may feel confident that they are linguistically qualified because of the informal endorsement by a colleague. This is not an appropriate seal of approval unless fluency can be corroborated professionally. Linguistic competence can be evaluated， and there is literature on the subject ， One’s claim of fluency can be immediately verified and simply cannot be feigned in the absence of true ability.**

【9】**Obtain Training**

**According to the ethical standards， psychologists must engage in profes-sional duties in new areas or involving new techniques only after first undertaking appropriate study， training， supervision， and/or consult-ing from persons who are competcnt in those areas or techniques"|删除换行|(1.04b). In the case of an emerging area in which no generally recog-nized training standards exist， they must “take reasonable steps to ensure the competence of their work and to protect patients， clients， students， research participants， and others from harm”(1.04c).**

【11】**Where language is concerned， psychologists who do not possess an adequate level of fluency， but who still wish to work with non-English-speaking populations， simply need to obtain the necessary training. Language classes， tutoring， and immersion programs are plentiful. Professionals need simply to take advantage of them. Training is also necessary beyond language. Familiarity with specific cultural idiosyn-crasies of the target population is an essential building block for compe-tence in the assessment of the poorly educated.The profound effects of schooling， and more specifically Western schooling， on tests of cogni-tive ability， are very well-documented in a large body of literature gener-ated by the field of cross-cultural psychology . In fact， familiarization with the work of Sylvia Scribner and Michael Cole (together and separately) should pro-vide a good start. In the case of illiterate patienus， the use of Western tests should be entertained with extreme caution and with complete awareness that the risk of misdiagnosis is very high. The reader may wish to consult Michael Cole's (1999) work for some suggestions on how a non-Western Binet may go about constructing tesis that may mea-sure aspects of cognition that are relevant to the particular non-Western society. Victor Nell’s _(2000) book， Cross Cultural Neuropsychological_ Assessment， provides an excellent background on the theoretical founda-tions of cross-cultural assessment and gives useful suggestions to those who may wish to practice it. Knowledge of this literature will assist the clinician in making decisions regarding the appropriateness of existing neuropsychological tests for assessment of individuals with very low lev-els of education or no education at all. Even more basically， a solid knowledge of the relevant aspects of the field of cultural anthropology is recommended， This field has concerned itself for many decades with literacy and formal schooling in various societies around the globe， and can provide the neuropsychologist with good insight and judgment vis-a-vis assessinent of individuals with low or no education.**

【12】**Maintain Language Skills**

**When a neuropsychologist possesses advanced fluency in a particular language， it must be kept in mind that， like any other skill， fluency declines over time without work and commitment to sustain it. It is|删除0换行|mandated that neuropsychologists “undertake ongoing efforts to main-tain competence in the skills they use”(1.05). Fluent clinicians should therefore be working to maintain language skills in all five modalities by speaking， listening， writing， reading， and thinking at an advanced level in the language， on a regular， even daily， basis.**

【14】**Ensure Linguistic and Cultural Competence of Subordinates**

【15】**Psychologists are also responsible for verifying the linguistic skills of any subordinates involved in the assessment procedure. The neuropsychol-ogist must delegate responsibility to individuals only when “such per-sons can reasonably be expected to perform competently， on the basis of their education， training， or experience"(1.22a). This standard is directly relevant to the use of translators， interpreters， or bilingual tech-nicians. It is clearly not enough， for example， for a monolingual English-speaking clinician to be satisfied that an assistant is bilingual based only on that individual's claim. The clinician is ultimately accountable.**

【16】**Refer if not Fluent**

【17】**Psychologists should “arrange for appropriate consultations and refer-rals based principally on the best interests of their patients or clients”(1.20a). This occurs quite readily in the profession whenever aclinician believes the client would be betier served by referral to， or collabora-tion with， another professional. In the case of a patient who is from a country with a variety of different languages (e.g.， China， India)， it is important that the clinician refer to another neuropsychologist who is fluent in the patient's specific language. Failure to make a referral when the neuropsychologist does not possess linguistic and cultural compe-tence adequate to meet the demands of cognitive assessment， and when another neuropsychologist who does possess such competence is avail~able， violates the spirit of this standard.**

**There will be cases in which no fluent bilingual clinician is available. Fowever， it is never acceptable for a neuropsychologist to simply assume this. Rather， he or she must always have current information about which colleagues in the geographic area are fluent. This informa-tion undergoes constant change as new clinicians become licensed and others may become adequately trained in a second language. Even if a linguistically qualified clinician is a considerable distance away， that option should be made available to both the patient and the referral source. The concerned neuropsychologist may also collaborate with a|删除0换行|bilingual psychologist in planning and carrying out the assessment. Approaching national or international neuropsychological associa-tions for names of colleagues who claim fluency in other languages is also a possibility， as is seeking the guidance and assistance of a col-league from the patient's country or linguistic group of origin through the internet.**

【19】**The clinician's ability to locate a fuent colleague clearly depends on how common the language of the patient is. In the event of a highly urcommon language， use of an interpreter may be unavoidable. The neuropsychologist is obligated to locate an interpreter， ideally with for-mal professional training and established competence. If a professional interpreter is not available， the next choice might be another individual with advanced fluency， such as a university language professor or some-one schooled in the assessment language through the university level. An interpreter should neuer be used when there is a fluent neuropsy-chologist or psychologist available， and no clinician with less than advanced fluency should ever assess unassisted. Convenient bystanders， such as friends or relatives of the patient or facility staff members， should not be considered as options under any circumstances because of the potential to contaminate data collcction in ways that the neuro psychologist cannot appreciate.**

【20】**Base All Statements on Verifiable Evidence**

【21】**Neuropsychologists’ “assessments， recommendations， reports， and psy-chological diagnostic or evaluative statements are based on information and techniques (including personal interviews of the individual when appropriate) sufficient to provide appropriate substantiation for their findings”(201b). Also， a psychologist's use of all techniques， interviews， and instruments is done “in a manner and for purposes that are appro-priate in light of the research on or evidence of the usefulness and prop-er application of the techniques”(2.02a).**

**Clinicians must be aware of the origin of any diagnostic measure used， including information on the standardization sample and the instrument's reliability and validity. This is particularly important when considering the use of translated instruments.“Bootleg”translations of standardized measures are in circulation， and the language used in many is of extremely poor quality . For this reason， unpublished instruments should never be employed unless there is powerful justification for doing so. Even when instru ments have been published， the clinician should critically appraise their|删除0换行|quality before using them. This goes for the instrument's psychometric qualities as well as its linguistic ardequacy， and this applies to both verbal and non-verbal instruments.**

【23】**With non-English-speaking populations who bave very little educa-tion， the challenges are not just linguistic； they embrace all other aspects of behavior. Errors can also occur when one assumes that non-linguistic aspects of cognition will be identical to those observed in the mainstream United States population. The contribution of lack of familiarity with testing situations in general and the perception of the clinician as a figure of power and authority who cannot be challenged may be important variables affecting the results with an examinee who has very little formal education.**

【24】**For non-English-speaking clients with higher levels of educational attainment， the bilingual clinician who chooses to assess may stand on slightly more solid ground. Indeed， based on preliminary data collected by the present author， for some tests at least， such individuals appear to obtain similar results to those of monolingual English speakers. However， even when education level is not an issue， normative data for non-English-speaking populations is scant. For some populations， normative informa-tion may be available in the patient's country of origin (e.g.， Italy) and the clinician is encouraged to contact scientists or practitioners in that coun~try to consult on availability of tests and guidelines for administration.**

【25】**In some cases， the referral source may be interested in specific diagnostic information， such as the presence or absence of brain damage after craniocerebral trauma or toxic exposure， or the presence of a dementing process versus depression. Diagnostic conclusions based on test performance of non-English speakers may be highly inappropri ate， particularly if there are no demographically adequate normative data available. If severe brain injury is suspected， neuroimaging data and examination by a neurologist will likely be far more valid than any results obtained through such questionable psychometric and other clinical practices. If the severity， or even the existence， of an insult can-not be based on verifiable evidence， clinicians should avoid making diagnostic statements altogether. They should， in fact， usually decline to assess linguistic minorities whenever the referral question is one seek-ing diagnostic information. Where low education errors are concerned， ignorance and poor judgment are implicated. It is likely that most neu-ropsychologists are aware that level of education has a profound effect on cognitive test performance.Therefore， those who ignore such infor-mation do so at great risk to their patients as well as to their own profes-sional reputations.**

【26】**If the clinician still wishes to conduct an evaluation in the absence of demographically and linguistically relevant normative data， it is advis-able not to administer any tests. In such a situation， it is recommended that the clinician take a thorough personal and social history from the patient and， from collateral sources， carefully study all available medical records. Then， make only tentative conclusions based on the history and what is known about the natural progression of the disease/injury in question. The clinician must always specify the fragility of his or her position in the report. Conclusions regarding motivation， level of coop-eration， guardedness， and other aspects of the clinical presentation must be carefully weighed. Ultimately， it is up to the clinician to educate referral sources about the limitations and appropriate uses of diagnos-tic tools. Referring professionals may incorrectly assume that a neu~ropsychological diagnostic evaluation is feasible for a particular patient for whom appropriate normative data do not exist. It is our responsibility to firmly decline referrals to test such patients.**

【27】**In other cases， the referral source may be less interested in a diagnosis than in a determination of the patient's functional ability in a particular English-language setting (e.g.， school， rehabilitation program place-ment， or vocational retraining). Responding to such a referral question may be entirely possible. In such situations， and provided the patient does possess sufficient English fluency to justify test administration， it may be appropriate to assess the patient's scholastic skills as well as abili-ties to learn material presented in English. Here， the clinician must ensure that the report of neuropsychological evaluation indicates clear-ly that the conclusions are not meant as a diagnosis， but merely as an assessment of the individual relative to inainstream individuals with oth-erwise similar demographic characteristics. Regardless of how a clini-cian decides to proceed， he or she should clearly state in the report the limitations of the following： the techniques and measures used， the normative comparisons made， and the confidence of interpretive state-ments. These caveats are essential in order to communicate the degree of confidence that one may have in the assessment and its findings. Obviously， if the number of caveats renders the report useless， it is better not to conduct the assessment in the first place. Furthermore， whenever the language used in the assessment is other than English， this information should also be provided in the report， as well as the specific qualifications of anyone who assisted in the evaluation.**

**Whenever an evaluation of this sort is initiated， the clinician should obtain informed consent from the patient. This should consisi of a clear written statement that includes the limitations outlined in the|删除0换行|preceding paragraph and information on the level of linguistic fluency of the clinician (including educational achievement in that language). If the clinician has anything less than the fluency of an educated native， the consent should outline the risks involved， such as the possibility of inaccurate diagnosis due to linguistic difficulty. The consent should specify that the patient was informed about the location of the nearest trained neuropsychologist with advanced native fluency， regardless of how far away that professional is， in order to demonstrate that the patient made an informed choice to proceed. This information should also be provided to the referral source at the time of referral. Informed consent. as usual， serves as a protection for both the patient and clinician.**

【223】**Clinical Manifestations of Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage**

**The onset of intraparenchymal hemorrhage is most often dur-ing wakefulness as a patient pursues the usual activities of|删除0换行|daily living. Maneuvers that cause a sudden rise in blood pres-sure such as heavy lifting， coitus， prolonged vomiting， cough-ing or straining at stool have been noted to cause hemorrhage with increased frequency. Unusual causes of hemorrhage are related to specific circumstances. Approximately 30% of ICH from aneurysm， AVM， and cavernous angioma occur during sleep.**

【225】**Most patients when first examined are alert (50%) with the remaining being lethargic (25%)， stuporous or comatose(25%). The onset is gradual over minutes to hours and the neurologic deficit is steadily progressive. CT and MRI serial evaluations have demonstrated that expansion occurs in the first 6 hours in approximately 20% of patients while 15%ex-pand during the next 6-12 hours and 6% between 6-24 hours. Expansion may be dramatic. In patients who suffer hemor-rhage from a bleeding diathesis expansion may occur insidi-ously over days.**

【226】**Focal deficits and consciousness are preserved at the ic-tus. Headache and vomiting may be absent. In subarachnoid hemorrhage， headache is severe， reaches maximum intensity almost instantly and focal neurologic signs are minimal. Loss of consciousness in SAH is much more frequent at the ictus than that which occurs with intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Embolism produces the greatest neurologic deficit at onset， is accompanied by a higher percentage of seizures than ICH and a lesser degree of headache. Patients who suffer emboli， particularly to the stem of the left MCA appear stunned. Is-chemic vascular disease is more frequent during sleep or the early moming and is accompanied frequently with deficits of a cortical nature such as aphasia or denial of contralateral space. Headache is common in ischemic disease with poste-rior circulation ischemia causing it more frequently than that from the anterior circulation. Rarely is it a predominant fea-ture.**

**Headache from intraparenchymal lesions occurs fre-quently as the hematoma develops and stretches the overlying dura， displaces the sinuses and major blood vessels at the base of the brain or spills into the subarachnoid space. Early in the course of the hemorrhage， the stretched dura may project pain to the overlying skull and scalp but most often the headache is projected frontally. The anterior and middle fossa dura and the forehead are innervated by V1 (somatic visceral con-vergence) and thus lesions in these fossa project to somatic representations of V1. Displacement of the posterior 1/3 of the sagittal sinus may also cause frontal headache. The dura of the posterior fossa is innervated by the posterior roots of C1-C2 and cranial nerves IX and X. Hematomas in the pos-terior fossa usually project pain to the basiocciput， posterior cervical areas or the trapezius ridge. They may project to the brow， the somatic representation of C2. Displacement of the tentorium and irritation of it’s under surface (innervated by C1-C2， IX and X) may cause pain in the inner ear. The upper leaflet of the tentorium is innervated by V1. Many patients who have suffered an intraparenchymal bleed are too lethar-gic to describe their headache accurately. Headache is most|删除0换行|common with lobar and cerebellar hematomas due to their close approximation to the dura and may be accompanied by signs of meningeal irritation. Headache increases with hematoma enlargement and is associated with vomiting and deterioration of the level of consciousness. Head tilt to the side of the hematoma， unilateral forced eye closure (ipsilat-eral to the side of the hematoma) and C2 headache are most suggestive of a cerebellar hemorrhage.**

【228】**Severe neck stiffness， photophobia， sore eyes， Brudzin-ski and Kerning’s signs suggest caudate hemorrhage with di-rect rupture into the ventricular system. Hyperthermia， rarely greater than 103° may be present. Thalamic and cerebellar hemorrhage may also be associated with early ventricular ex-tension. Larger putaminal hemorrhages rarely rupture into the ventricular system at onset.**

【229】**The focal deficits and topography of each type of hem-orrhage will be described in detail. Specific neurological deficits suggest a characteristic hemorrhage： (1) a deeply co-matose patient with head and eyes deviated to the side of the lesion， a flaccid hemiparesis and hemisensory defect with periodic breathing is characteristic of a deep pallidal hem-orrhage； (2) inability to walk， dysarthria， nystagmus with quadriparesis not plegia suggests a cerebellar hemorrhage；(3) a patient whose eyes are down and in with a greater sen-sory than motor deficit is sentinel for a thalamic bleed； (4) an elderly patient with arm， face weakness who has suffered a seizure suggests a lobar congophilic hemorrhage.**

【230】**Vomiting and nausea may occur at the ictus of an intra-parenchymal hemorrhage due to the sudden increase of ICP that is transmitted to the mechanosensitive emetic center of the floor of the IV ventricle or distortion of the IV ventri-cle itself. Vomiting stops as pressure is relieved by displace-ment of CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space， overbreath-ing that effects a decrease of pCOz and consequent reduc-tion of cerebral blood flow as well as intracranial shifts of brain parenchyma. As the hematoma expands further， vom-iting and nausea return due to exhaustion of compensatory mechanisms.**

**Persistent vomiting out of proportion to dizziness is sug-gestive of an ischemic lesion of the brainstem. Vomiting with change of head position is characteristic of a mass in the IVth ventricle. Inability to vomit in the face of a strong urge to do so is characteristic of an intrinsic medullary lesion. A smooth gradual deterioration of neurological function over minutes to hours with concomitant headache and vomiting is most consistent with supratentorial intraparenchymal hem-orrhage. Headaches are most often seen with larger hemor-rhages whereas deep parenchymal lesions may be asymp-tomatic. Approximately 30% of patients suffer headaches at the ictus， another 20% develop it during evolution of their neurologic deficits and up to 40% may have no headache. Many of the latter patients are lethargic or obtunded at the time of evaluation. Lobar and cerebellar hemorrhages have the highest incidence of headaches due to their proximity to the meninges. 【31】Keep in mind that the causes of dizziness may overlap the different subtypes. Some patients cannot describe their symp-toms in a way that fits neatly into the 4 subtypes. Half of elderly patients describe 2 or more dizziness subtypes. Psy-chiatrie causes often coexist with other causes of dizziness.12Dysequilibrium may follow disorders that produce vertigo. Vestibular neuronitis or labyrinthitis initially presents with vertigo but may subsequently cause unsteadiness in the legs(dysequilibrium) lasting for several weeks or months. Like-wise， vertebrobasilar stroke can present with vertigo followed by dysequilibrium because some patients (particularly the elderly) may also have reduced compensatory multisensory and circulatory systems.

【32】See the algorithms  for evaluating patients with dizziness and assessing those with vertigo.

【33】·AA single etiology may result in more than 1 subtype of dizziness.

【34】· Positional vertigo may be confused with postural hypo-tension. Both can occur on arising； however， positional vertigo occurs with a change in position that does not result in global cerebral hypoperfusion. For example， positional vertigo (but not postural hypotension) may oc-cur with rolling over in bed or bending forward to put on socks or tie shoes.

【35】Although uncommon， cerebellar stroke may present only with vertigo and ataxia and thus be mistaken for vestibular neuronitis. The ataxia is severe， and most patients are unable to walk without support. Acute onset and atherosclerotic risk factors should heighten clinical suspicion.

【13】**Presyncope/Syncope**

【14】In a dizzy patient who has lost consciousness， syncope must be distinguished from seizure. See Chapter 29 for the diagnos-tic approach to presyncope/syncope.

【15】**Dysequilibrium**

【16】Visual impairment， hearing loss， peripheral neuropathy， and musculoskeletal abnormalities all contribute to the syndrome of multiple sensory deficits， which is a common geriatric syndrome. Ask specific questions to further delineate any sen-sory and/or motor impairment.

| **Are you having any trouble seeing?**  | **Visual impairment (eg， cataract)**  |

| **Do you feel weak in your legs or haveincoordination in your legs?**  | **Musculoskeletal abnormalities (eg， cervical spondylosis， osteoarthritis，cervicogenic dizziness accompanied by headache)， cerebellardysfunction， spinal stenosis， spinal cord disorders， movement disorders** **(eg， Parkinson’s disease)**  |

【25】**Light-headedness (Undifferentiated Dizziness)**

【26】Frequently， underlying psychological disorders are associated with this subtype of dizziness， which is difficult for patients to describe. In addition， prescription drug toxicity and substance abuse are associated with this subtype.

【27】Four clinical cues (S4 model) predict a subgroup of ambulatory patients likely to have underlying depressive and anxiety disorders. The presence of 2 or more of these clini-cal cues signals the need for a more detailed psychological evaluation.

【28】**S4 Model (Cues： Symptom Count， Stress， Severity， Self-Rated Health)"**

【31】Keep in mind that the causes of dizziness may overlap the different subtypes. Some patients cannot describe their symp-toms in a way that fits neatly into the 4 subtypes. Half of elderly patients describe 2 or more dizziness subtypes. Psy-chiatrie causes often coexist with other causes of dizziness.12Dysequilibrium may follow disorders that produce vertigo. Vestibular neuronitis or labyrinthitis initially presents with vertigo but may subsequently cause unsteadiness in the legs(dysequilibrium) lasting for several weeks or months. Like-wise， vertebrobasilar stroke can present with vertigo followed by dysequilibrium because some patients (particularly the elderly) may also have reduced compensatory multisensory and circulatory systems.

【32】See the algorithms  for evaluating patients with dizziness and assessing those with vertigo.

【33】·AA single etiology may result in more than 1 subtype of dizziness.

【34】· Positional vertigo may be confused with postural hypo-tension. Both can occur on arising； however， positional vertigo occurs with a change in position that does not result in global cerebral hypoperfusion. For example， positional vertigo (but not postural hypotension) may oc-cur with rolling over in bed or bending forward to put on socks or tie shoes.

【35】Although uncommon， cerebellar stroke may present only with vertigo and ataxia and thus be mistaken for vestibular neuronitis. The ataxia is severe， and most patients are unable to walk without support. Acute onset and atherosclerotic risk factors should heighten clinical suspicion.

【21】LAQUES of mycosis fungoides and1papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have many features in common， among them the presence of atypical lymphocytes， epidermotropism of lympho-cytes， atypical lymphocytes arranged both as solitary units and in collections within the epidermis， lymphocytes aligned in the basal layer of the epider-mis sometimes， lymphocytes in the epidermis larger than some of them within the dermis， a psoriasiform or psoriasiform lichenoid pattern， an infiltrate of lymphocytes that is mostly superficial， lymphocytes sometimes situated in the upper reaches of the epidermis including the cornified layer， intraepidermal collections of lymphocytes that vary in size， epithelial struc-tures of adnexa permeated by lymphocytes sometimes， wiry bundles of col-lagen in haphazard array in the papillary dermis at times， and coarse bun-dles of collagen in vertical streaks in a thickened papillary dermis (lichen simplex chronicus). In some specimens， atypical lymphocytes in both dis-eases may be confined wholly to the dermis with no evidence of epider-motropism.

Mycosis fungoides in the plaque stage can be differentiated histopatho-logically from adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in the papular stage by both architectural and cytologic features. Cytologically， lymphocytes in mycosis fungoides have less cytoplasm， are relatively monomorphous， are more cer-ebriform (and more of them are cerebriform)， and are not associated with abundant nuclear “dust.” The latter finding reflects the fact that lympho-cytes in mycosis fungoides do not undergo necrosis readily. Furthermore， eosinophils are present commonly within plaques of mycosis fungoides， but not in papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Although both plaques of mycosis fungoides and papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma may be associated with prominent collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis， large collections of them are much more common in leukemia/lymphoma (where there are many more of them). Even when collections of atypical lymphocytes form within the epidermis of plaques of mycosis fun-goides， the collections tend to be small and usually seem insignificant in comparison with the atypical lymphocytes that pepper the epidermis as solitary units. In adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma， collections of atypical lymphocytes tend to predominate over atypical lymphocytes arranged as solitary units within the epidermis. Because plaques of mycosis fungoides are long-standing by the time that they come to be biopsied， in contrast to papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma that are relatively short-lived at the time they are sampled by biopsy， differences in quantity of wiry bundles of collagen in the thickened papillary dermis are to be expected. In mycosis|删除0换行|fungoides， extensive repiacement of the normal papillary dermis by wiry collagen bundles in haphazard array is common， whereas those alterations， when they are present at all in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma，are subtle. Another sign of chronicity in plaques of mycosis fungoides is absence of edema from the papillary dermis； edema in papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma indicates acutcness of thatprocess.

【23】Just as patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides share many histo-oathologic features with patients who havepapules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma， so， too， it is for clinical lesions of those diseases. Both diseases may be constituted of macules， papules， patches， plaques， nodules， tumors， and ulcerated tumors. Patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides， however， may exhibit discrete plaques only， and not a potpourri of other cutaneous lesions. In contrast， patients with papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma almost always have numerous nodules， too. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually favor the buttocks and the trunk. Papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have a predilection for the extremities， which may become markedly edematous. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually do not ulcerate， whereasSpapules and nodules of adult T-cellleukemia/lymphoma may ulcerate and be covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Whereas patches and plaques tend to predominate in mycosis fungoides， papules usually predominate in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Papules are un-common in mycosis fungoides.

【24】The cause of mycosis fungoides is not known. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma has been demonstrated to be a lympho-proliferative disorder induced by a type C retrovirus (HTLV-3). In short， it is a T-cell lymphoma with a fulminant， fatal course. Multilobulated lymphocytes in the peripheral blood are markers of the disease. Those lymphocytes usually are of the T-helper/inducer immunophenotype， just as are those of mycosis fungoides.

【25】Plaques of mycosis fungoides signify that the disease has been present in the skin for many years before a patient has come to a physician. At that time， cutaneous manifestations of mycosis fungoides may be the only ex-pressions of the disease； no internal ones may be discernible. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemialymphoma develops rapidly， and when patients see a physician， they not only have cutaneous manifestations， but lymphadenopa-thy， hepatosplenomegaly， and pulmonary involvement by the lymphoma-tous process. Hypercalcemia is frequent in patients with adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma.

【26】Histopathologic findings in plaques of mycosis fungoides and in pap-ules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma are startlingly similar， but they can be differentiated if heed is paid to the criteria set forth in this chapter.

【76】Amajor trial for histopathologists may be posed by differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicu-lar lymphoma. The reasons are obvious. Even pseudolymphomas devoid of lymphoid follicles may confound histopathologists who seek to differentiate them from malignant lymphomas. That difficulty is compounded when lymphoid follicles， reputed to be a sign of pseudolymphomas， are present in authentic lymphomas. The follicular lymphoma under discussion in this chapter is a B-cell lymphoma.

【77】At the outset， a clear distinction must be made between primary and secondary lymphoid follicles. The attributes of those two structures are based upon findings in normal lymph nodes. Primary follicles are those in which lymphocytes have monomorphous nuclei， and secondary follicles are those that contain germinal centers. In this discussion of criteria for histo-pathologic differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicular lymphoma， secondary follicles alone are germane.

【78】Common to both pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles and follicu-lar lymphoma are dense nodular or diffuse predominantly lymphocytic in-filtrates within the dermis and， often， within the subcutaneous fat， lymph-oid follicleswithin the dermis andsometimes the subcutaneousfat， lymphocytes in mitosis， at least two populations of lymphocytes， na small and large ones， and absence of epidermal involvement.

It is well known to dermatopathologists that， in attempting to distin-guish infiltrates of lymphocytes in inflammatory diseases that simulate lym-phomas from those in true lymphomas， criteria cmployed for that purpose are flawed， sometimes seriously. When all， or nearly all， of the findings listed at the outset of this chapter are found in a particular section of skin， a diagnosis of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles or follicular lym-phoma usually can be made readily. All too often， however， that good for-tune for a histopathologist is not the case， and， in those instances where a specific diagnosis is not apparent at first glance， an orderly method based upon a catechism must be applied diligently. That method utilizes architec-SPSS6tural pattern， as assessed at scanning magnification， as the surest route to differentiation betweenbenign and malignant neoplasms in general and between inflammatoryinfiltrates of lymphocytes in nodular and diffuse array， i.e.， pseudolymphomas， from authentic lymphomas in particular. The crucial attributes for a histopathologist to assess are where in the skin the infiltration of lymphocytes is most dense (“top-heavy”as in pseudolym-phomas or “bottom-heavy”as in lymphomas)， what shape does the infil-trate assume (wedge-shaped as is the case for some pseudolymphomas， or|删除0换行|not as in lymphomas)， how dense is the infiltrate (dense but not massive as in pseudolymphomas or massive sometimes as in lymphomas)， and how deep is the infiltrate (not simply into subcutaneous fat， as occurs in both pseudo- and lymphomas， but into skeletal muscles as happens only in lym-phomas as a rule). At higher magnifications， the decisive features that en-able distinction between the inflammatory and neoplastic process include“tingible bodies” (present commonly in germinal centers of pseudolympho-mas， but not in lymphomas)， striking pleomorphism of nuclei of lympho-cytes (pleomorphic in germinal centers of pseudolymphomas， but not out-side of those centers as they are in lymphomas)， and well-defined mantles of lymphocytes around germinal centers (prominent cuffs of lymphocytes are present in pseudolymphomas， but are ill-defined in lymphomas). These sets of distinguishing characteristics， when present in constellation， permit pseudolymphomas with lymphoid follicles to be discriminated from follicu-lar lymphomas in most instances.

【80】Similarities between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma exist clinically. Both the inflammatory and neoplastic processes are characterized clinicallv by painless papules， plaques， nodules， or tumors that vary in size and in color from red to violaceous. Both occur commonly on the head and neck. The presence of tumors of gigantic proportions favors a diagnosis of lym-phoma. As is true of malignant neoplasms in general， lymphomas continue to grow relentlessly； pseudolymphomas stop growing or even regress.

【81】Immunoperoxidase techniques may clarify the nature of an infiltrate of lymphocytes with associated follicles. The same principles that govern dif-ferentiation ofpseudolymphoma from lymphoma in sections stained by hematoxylin and eosin obtain equally for sections stained by immunoperox-idase techniques， to wit， a mixedpopulation favors pseudolymphoma， and a monomorphous population of llymphocytes favors lymphoma. Follicular lymphomas， being B-cell lymphomas， stain with B-cell markers in both lymphoid follicles and the interfollicular dermis and subcutaneous fat. Pseudolymphomnas tend to reproduce the normal architecture of a lymph node， i.e.， B-cells predominate in germinal centers， and T-cells predominate in the dermis between lymphoid follicles.

【82】Another difference between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma is re-vealed when immunoperoxidase techniques are used to detect expression of surface immunoglobulins. Lymphocytes of a pseudolymphoma express a mixture of lambda and kappa light chains. Lymphomas， on the contrary， express only one light chain or neither of them.

【83】Unfortunately， no matter what studies are performed， dense nodular and/or diffuse infiltrates of lymphocytes， with or without lymphoid follicles， may defy identification by current methods. In those situations， and if le-sions persist， additional biopsies should be taken over time and the patient followed carefully for signs of systemic manifestations of lymphoma.

【99】RITERIA for differentiation of xanthogranuloma from necrobiotic xanthogranuloma pertain to lesions of xanthogranuloma that are fully developed and of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma that are still evolving. These two conditions， at those different stages in their evolution， may be confused with one another because they have so many histopatho-logic features in common： predominance， or near predominance， of foam cells over other types of inflammatory cells； presence of Touton giant cells； mixed-cell infiltrates that contain lymphocytes， plasma cells， cosinophils， and histiocytes； extensive fibrosis； involvement of the subcutaneous fat； sparing of epidermis； and location， sometimes， on skin damaged badly by sunlight. It is important to identify these two conditions for what they are because they are so different biologically.

【100】Xanthogranuloma in skin affects children and adults differently. Histo-pathologically， however， the “juvenile" and “adult”types are indistinguish-able from one another. At an early stage， both are characterized by diffuse infiltrates of oval-shaped histiocytes in the upper part of the dermis. Mitotic figures may be present in those rapidly proliferating histiocytes marked sometimes by pleomorphic nuclei， and the lesion， at that stage， even may be misinterpreted as that of a carcinoma or sarcoma. In time， the cytoplasm of the histiocytes becomes increasingly foamy， Touton giant cells appear within the infiltrate， and the lesion is sprinkled with neutrophils， eosino-phils， lymphocytes， andplasma cells. Eventually，a cutaneousXan-thogranuloma undergoes regression by fibrosis.

【101】**Despite the fact that “juvenile”and “adult”expressions of cutaneous xanthogranuloma are indistinguishable from one another histopathologi-cally， they are different from one another clinically and biologically. Cutane-ous xanthogranuloma in adults presents itself usually as a solitary lesion and， nearly always， is not associated with xanthogranulomas in any other organ. In contrast， xanthogranulomas in children tend to be multiple and involve other organs such as the eyes， lungs， bones， kidneys， pericardium， colon， overies， and testes. Lesions of juvenile xanthogranuloma have been associated at times with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromatoses. When an eye is affected by xanthogranuloma in a child， bleeding can occur and blind-ness may result. Xanthogranulomas in children and adults， because of their abundant lipid， appear clinically as yellow or yellow-orangc lesions. The clinical differential diagnosis of juvenile xanthogranuloma is nodular lesions of mastocytosis in children. Unlike the situation in adults， in whom a lesion of xanthogranuloma does not revert， the lesions in children involute.**

【102】**Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma usually affects persons who have passed the age of 50. The disease presents itself as papules and plaques， often on the periorbital areas of the face but also on the trunk and extremities， that tend to ulcerate. On the face， papules may become confluent and extend into an eye with resultant uveitis， iritis， and keratitis. On extremities， a lesion may resemble necrobiosis lipoidica closely. When a diagnosis of nec-robiotic xanthogranuloma has been established on histopathologic grounds， search must be undertaken for evidence of associated paraproteinemia with an IgG monoclonal gammopathy. In about one third of patients， a diagnosis of multiple mycloma is apparent from the outset. The disease progresses slowly to a fatal outcome.**

【103】**Histopathologically， as necrobiotic xanthogranuloma progresses be-yond the findings described at the outset of this chapter， the condition comes to resemble a caricature of necrobiosis lipoidica. When fully devel-oped， the process involves the entire dermis and much of the subcutaneous fat in the form of large zones of degeneration of collagen， within which there may be numerous cholesterol clefts and deposits of calcium. Zones of degenerated collagen often are surrounded by numerous foamy histiocytes that cnable necrobiotic xanthogranuloma to be differentiated from necrobi-osis lipoidica， in which there are none. Foam cells and calcification are consequences of necrosis of adipocytes in the subcutaneous fat. Lympho-plasmocytic infiltrates， like those in necrobiosis lipoidica， are present throughout the dermis and the subcutaneous fat. Findings in fully developed lesions of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma are specific for that condition.**

Low-grade surface osteosarcoma is usually termed parosteal osteosarcoma. The lesion arises on the outside surface of the bone， virtually never pro-voking a periosteal reaction (361，418，431). Histologi-cally， the proliferating portion of the neoplasm consists of a fibrous stroma， considered to be derived from the outer fibrous periosteal laver. Dedifferentiated parosteal osteosarcoma is a high-grade variant of the former tu-mor (393，455). Periosteal osteosarcoma belongs to an intermediate grade of surface lesions (434). This lesion may cause periosteal response and usually consists mostly of cartilage (381). The lesion is believed to be de-rived from the inner， or cambium， layer of periosteum. High-grade surface osteosarcoma is a lesion located on the periphery of a bone. It has a histology identical to that of conventional medullary osteosarcoma and a simi-lar metastatic potential (363，454，460).

【5】**_Parosteal Osteosarcoma_**

【6】This type of surface osteosarcoma， which accounts for about 4% of all osteosarcomas， is seen in patients in their third and fourth decades， and characteristically affects the posterior aspect of the distal femur (414). Other locations include the tibia， the fibula， and the proximal portions of the femur and humerus(331). Rarely are other bones affected (306，312). Be-cause the tumor is slow growing and usually involves only the surface of the bone， the prognosis is much better than for the other types of osteosarcoma.

【7】On radiologic studies， the neoplasm presents as a dense oval or spherical mass attached to the surface of the cortical bone . The surface is lobulated and may be less dense than the base of the tumor . The mass appears sharply delineated from the peripheral soft tissues. The medullary cavity is usually spared unless the lesion is of long duration. A linear， translucent cleft usually forms an incomplete separa-tion of the bulk of the tumor from the underlying cortex . Larger lesions， however， tend to en-circle the host bone (361). Although these features can be adequately demonstrated by conventional radiogra-phy， CT  or MRI  is often neces-sary to determine the extent of cortical penetration and intramedullary invasion by tumor (295).

【8】The histology of this tumor is characterized by a high degree of structural differentiation and consists of im-mature (woven) bone in different stages of maturation to lamellar bone (395). The lamellar trabeculae， which predominate in most areas， are separated by a bland， well-differentiated fibrous stroma composed of spindle cells. The latter show minimal cytologic atypia， are mini-mally pleomorphic， and rarely exhibit mitotic activity. The surface may be covered by hyper-cellular and slightly atypical cartilage mimicking osteo-chondroma . Cartilaginous tumor nodules may also be present within the lesion. Determining ma-lignancy may present some difficulty， as the indolent na-ture of this tumor is also evidenced by lack of significant tumor hemorrhage or necrosis. Then， either sponta-neously (in which case both low- and high-grade com-ponents can be identified histologically) or secondarily(in recurrences of inadequately resected low-grade parosteal tumors)， the lesion undergoes transforma-tion to a high-grade malignancy (367，452). The latter situation is more common. Unni (431) cites a dediffer-entiation rate of 20% in such recurrences. Only excep-tionally rare， as reported by Shuhaibar and Friedman(402)， the tumor at initial presentation shows coexis-tence of both the low-grade and high-grade sarcomas. In radiologic and histologic studies， dedifferentiated parosteal osteosarcoma mimics the features of conven-tional parosteal osteosarcoma. There are， however， some characteristics of a high-grade sarcoma， such as radiographically identifiable cortical destruction and histologically identifiable pleomorphic tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and a high mitotic rate. Cross-sectional imaging reveals medullary involvement in22% of patients and adjacent soft tissue invasion in46% (361) . Hence， the prognosis is much worse than for parosteal osteosarcoma.

【14】**_Periosteal Osteosarcoma_**

【15】This very rare type of osteosarcoma (accounting for1%-2% of all osteosarcomas and 25% of all surface os-teosarcomas) grows on the surface of a bone and is usu-ally located in the midshaft of a long bone； it is most common in adolescence (283). Although the age range varies， most lesions occur during the second decade of life. There is a slight female preponderance， and the ma-jority of lesions affect the tibia and femur (85%-95%) followed by the ulna and humerus (5%-10%)(351).

【16】The radiologic characteristics were defined by de-Santos et al. (250). These include heterogeneous tu-mor matrix with calcified spiculations interspersed with areas of radiolucency representing uncalcified matrix； occasional periosteal reaction in the form of a Codman triangle ； thickening of the periosteal sur-face of the cortex at the base of the lesion， with sparing of the endosteal surface； extension of the tumor into the soft tissues； and sparing of the medullary cavity.

【5】**_Parosteal Osteosarcoma_**

【6】This type of surface osteosarcoma， which accounts for about 4% of all osteosarcomas， is seen in patients in their third and fourth decades， and characteristically affects the posterior aspect of the distal femur (414). Other locations include the tibia， the fibula， and the proximal portions of the femur and humerus(331). Rarely are other bones affected (306，312). Be-cause the tumor is slow growing and usually involves only the surface of the bone， the prognosis is much better than for the other types of osteosarcoma.

【7】On radiologic studies， the neoplasm presents as a dense oval or spherical mass attached to the surface of the cortical bone . The surface is lobulated and may be less dense than the base of the tumor . The mass appears sharply delineated from the peripheral soft tissues. The medullary cavity is usually spared unless the lesion is of long duration. A linear， translucent cleft usually forms an incomplete separa-tion of the bulk of the tumor from the underlying cortex . Larger lesions， however， tend to en-circle the host bone (361). Although these features can be adequately demonstrated by conventional radiogra-phy， CT  or MRI  is often neces-sary to determine the extent of cortical penetration and intramedullary invasion by tumor (295).

【8】The histology of this tumor is characterized by a high degree of structural differentiation and consists of im-mature (woven) bone in different stages of maturation to lamellar bone (395). The lamellar trabeculae， which predominate in most areas， are separated by a bland， well-differentiated fibrous stroma composed of spindle cells. The latter show minimal cytologic atypia， are mini-mally pleomorphic， and rarely exhibit mitotic activity. The surface may be covered by hyper-cellular and slightly atypical cartilage mimicking osteo-chondroma . Cartilaginous tumor nodules may also be present within the lesion. Determining ma-lignancy may present some difficulty， as the indolent na-ture of this tumor is also evidenced by lack of significant tumor hemorrhage or necrosis. 【12】**_Dedifferentiated Parosteal Osteosarcoma_**

【13】Dedifferentiatedi parosteal _l_ osteosarcoma， the more common variant of surface-based high-grade osteosar-comas， usually arises aLsSaconventional low-grade parosteal osteosarcoma (455). Then， either sponta-neously (in which case both low- and high-grade com-ponents can be identified histologically) or secondarily(in recurrences of inadequately resected low-grade parosteal tumors)， the lesion undergoes transforma-tion to a high-grade malignancy (367，452). The latter situation is more common. Unni (431) cites a dediffer-entiation rate of 20% in such recurrences. Only excep-tionally rare， as reported by Shuhaibar and Friedman(402)， the tumor at initial presentation shows coexis-tence of both the low-grade and high-grade sarcomas. In radiologic and histologic studies， dedifferentiated parosteal osteosarcoma mimics the features of conven-tional parosteal osteosarcoma. There are， however， some characteristics of a high-grade sarcoma， such as radiographically identifiable cortical destruction and histologically identifiable pleomorphic tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and a high mitotic rate. Cross-sectional imaging reveals medullary involvement in22% of patients and adjacent soft tissue invasion in46% (361) . Hence， the prognosis is much worse than for parosteal osteosarcoma.

【14】**_Periosteal Osteosarcoma_**

【15】This very rare type of osteosarcoma (accounting for1%-2% of all osteosarcomas and 25% of all surface os-teosarcomas) grows on the surface of a bone and is usu-ally located in the midshaft of a long bone； it is most common in adolescence (283). Although the age range varies， most lesions occur during the second decade of life. There is a slight female preponderance， and the ma-jority of lesions affect the tibia and femur (85%-95%) followed by the ulna and humerus (5%-10%)(351).

【16】The radiologic characteristics were defined by de-Santos et al. (250). These include heterogeneous tu-mor matrix with calcified spiculations interspersed with areas of radiolucency representing uncalcified matrix； occasional periosteal reaction in the form of a Codman triangle ； thickening of the periosteal sur-face of the cortex at the base of the lesion， with sparing of the endosteal surface； extension of the tumor into the soft tissues； and sparing of the medullary cavity.

【0】o. During the course of the medical history， you notice that the client has a persistent cough and that he sounds hoarse，

【1】After reviewing the Personal/Family History form， you note that the client smokes two packs of cigarettes each day and that he has smoked at least this amount for at least 50years. (One pack per day for 1 year is considered “one pack-year.) This person has smoked an estimated 100 pack-years； anyone who has smoked for 20 pack-years or more is considered to be at risk for the development of serious lung disease.

【2】What questions will you ask to decide for yourself whether his back pain is systemic?

【3】**_introduction to Client_**

【4】It is important for me to make certain that your back pain is not caused by other health problems， such as prostate prob-lems or respiratory infection， so I will ask a series of questions that may not seem to be related to your back pain， but I want to be very thorough and cover every possibility to obtain the best and most effective t OU.reatment for you.

【5】**_Pain_**

【6】From your history form， I see that you associate your back pain with lifting a heavy box 2 weeks ago. When did you first notice your back pain (sudden or gradual onset)?

【7】Have you ever hurt your back before or have you ever had pain similar to this episode in the past? (Systemic disease：recurrent and gradually increases over time)

【8】Please describe your pain (supply descriptive terms if necessary).

【9】How often do you have this pain?

【10】Follow-ups (FUPs)： How long does it last when you have it? What aggravates your pain/symptoms?

【11】What relieves your pain/symptoms?

【12】How does rest affect your pain?

【13】Have you noticed any change in your pain/symptoms since they first started to the present time?

【14】Do you have any numbness in the groin or inside your legs?(Saddle anesthesia： cauda equina)

【15】**_Putmonary_**

【16】I notice you have quite a cough and you sound hoarse to me. How long have you had this cough and hoarseness (when did it first begin)?

【17】Do you have any back pain associated with this cough? Any other pain associated with your cough?

【18】Ifyes： Have the person describe where， when， intensity，aggra-vating and relieving factors.

【19】How does it feel when you take a deep breath? Does your low back hurt when you laugh or take a deep breath?

【20】When you cough， do you produce phlegm or mucus?

【21】If yes： Have you ever noticed any red streaks or blood in it?

【22】Does your coughing or back pain keep you awake at night?

【23】Have you been examined by a physician for either your cough or your back pain?

【24】Have you had any recent chest or spine x-rays taken?

【25】If yes： When and where? What were the results?

【26】**_General Systemic_**

【27】Have you had any night sweats， daytime fevers， or chills?

【28】Do you have difficulty in swallowing (Esophageal cancer， anxiety， cervical disc protrusion)?

【29】Have you had laryngitis over and over? (Oral cancer)

【30】**_Urologic_**

【31】Have you ever been told that you have a prostate problem or prostatitis?

【32】Ifyes： Determine when this occurred， how it was treated， and whether the person had the same symptoms at that time that he is now describing to you.

【33】Have you noticed any change in your bladder habits?

Follow-up questions (FUPS)： Have you had any difficulty|删除换行|in starting or continuing to urinate?

【35】Have you noticed any blood in your urine?

【36】Have you recently had any difficulty with kidney stones or bladder or kidney infections?

【37】**_Gastrointestinal_**

【38】Have you noticed any change in your bowel pattern?

【39】Have you had difficulty having a bowel movement?

【40】Do you find that you have soiled yourself without even real-izing it? (Cauda equina lesion-this would require imme-diate referral to a physician)

【41】Does your back pain begin or increase when you are having a bowel movement?

【42】Is your back pain relieved after having a bowel movement?

【43】Have you noticed any association between when you eat and when your pain/symptoms increase or decrease?

【44】**_Final Question_**

【45】Is there anything about your current back pain or your gen-eral health that we have not discussed that you think is important for me to know?

【141】**Screening for Gastrointestinal Disease**

【142】A great deal of new understanding of the enteric system and its relationship to other systems has been discovered over the last decade. For example， it is now known that the lining of the digestive tract from the esophagus through the large intestine  is composed of approximately 100 million nerve cells that contain neuropeptides and their receptors. This neural network has been called the enteric nervous sys-tem (ENS) and provides the connection between digestion， mood， and health.删除14:<u>1，2</u>

【143】In addition to the classic hormonal and neural negative feedback loops， there are direct actions of gut hormones on the dorsal vagal complex. The person experiencing aa“gut reaction”or “gut feeling” may indeed be experiencing the direct effects of gut peptides on brain function.

【144】The association between the enteric system， the immune system， and the brain (now a part of the research referred to as psychoneuroimmunology \[PNI\]) has been clearly estab-lished and forms an integral part of gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms associated with immune disorders such as fibro-myalgia， systemic lupus erythematosus， rheumatoid arthritis， and chronic fatigue syndrome.

【145】Researchers estimate that more than two thirds of all immune activity occurs in the gut. There are more T cells in the intestinal epithelium than in all other body tissues com-bined. The gamma delta T cells form the forefront of the immune defense mechanism. They act as an early warning system for the cells lining the intestines， which are heavily exposed to microorganisms and toxins. In some people the wall of the gut seems to have been breached， either because the network of intestinal cells develops increased perme-ability (a syndrome referred to as "leaky gut") or perhaps because bacteria and yeast overwhelm it and migrate into the bloodstream.删除14:<u>4</u>

【146】All of these associations and new findings support the need for the physical therapist to carefully assess the possibility of GI symptoms being present but unreported. This is especially important when considering the fact that GI tract problems can sometimes imitate musculoskeletal dysfunction.

【147】GI disorders can refer pain to the sternal region， shoulder and neck， scapular region， midback，lower back， hip， pelvis， and sacrum. This pain can mimic primary musculoskeletal or neuromuscular dysfunction， causing confusion for the physi-cal therapist or for the physician assessing the client’s chief complaints.

【148】Although these neuromusculoskeletal symptoms can occur alone and far from the actual site of the disorder， the client usually has other systemic signs and symptoms associ-ated with GI disorders that should give the therapist grounds for suspicion.

【149】A careful interview to screen for systemic illness should include a few important questions concerning the client’s his-tory， prescribed medications， and the presence of any asso-ciated signs or symptoms that would immediately alert the therapist to the need for medical follow-up. The most com-mon intraabdominal diseases that refer pain to the musculo-skeletal system are those that involve ulceration or infection of the mucosal lining. Drug-induced GI symptoms can also occur with delayed reactions as much as 6 or 8 weeks after exposure to the medication. The most common occurrences are antibiotic colitis； nausea， vomiting， and anorexia from digitalis toxicity； and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug(NSAID)-induced ulcers.

【110】**INTRODUCTION**

【111】Primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the testis is a rare dis-ease and accounts for ~9% of testicular tumors (but is the most common malignancy in elderly patients). Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)， the most common type of testicu-lar lymphoma， occurs mostly in patients >60 years old and is clinically characterized by unilateral painless scrotal swelling； high incidence of bilateral involvement (35%)； frequent spread to the skin， central nervous system (CNS)， lung， and Waldeyer’s ring； and aggressive clinical behavior with poor prognosis， especially in patients with advanced disease 通用删除6(英):<u>\[1-10\]</u>. Testis may be rarely involved by mantle cell lymphoma (MCL)， Burkitt lymphoma (BL)， peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL)， not oth-erwise specified， anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL)， and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma， nasal type (ENKTL).

【112】**B-CELL NEOPLASMS**

【113】**DIFFUSE LARGE B-CELL LYMPHOMA**

【114】**Introduction**

Primary testicular DLBCL has a poor prognosis despite localized presentation and doxorubicin-based chemotherapy通用删除6(英):<u>\[2，3，5，7，11\]</u>. Extratesticular dissemination (often to the CNS) is common. Adding the rituximab to the treatment protocol in|删除0换行|the last decade did not improve significantly disease-free sur-vival in patients with testicular DLBCL (as opposed to nodal disease， where there is a significant improvement in outcome after addition of rituximab). Approximately 50% of patients with testicular DLBCL present with stage II-IV disease 通用删除6(英):<u>\[7\]</u>. Touroutoglou et al. 通用删除6(英):<u>\[2\]</u> reported that the failure-free survival rate at 153 months was 16% for all patients or 32% and 0% for those with International Prognostic Index (IPI) scores ≤l and>l， respectively. The CNS or contralateral testis was involved in all patients who failed to respond to primary therapy and in 50% of those who relapsed from complete remission. In a series reported by Darby et al.， 40% of patients with testicu-lar lymphoma relapsed following a complete response and a median time to relapse was 9 months 通用删除6(英):<u>\[8\]</u>. Only one of these relapses was in the CNS， one in the bone， one in the skin， and two in the contralateral testis. The majority of relapses (58%) occurred in the lymph nodes.

【116】**Cytogenetics/FISH**

The study by Bosga-Bouwer et al. 通用删除6(英):<u>\[12\]</u> suggested that 6q dele-tions play a major pathogenetic role in DLBCL of the testis and that many of these deletions are part of unbalanced transloca-tions. 【110】**INTRODUCTION**

【111】Primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the testis is a rare dis-ease and accounts for ~9% of testicular tumors (but is the most common malignancy in elderly patients). Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)， the most common type of testicu-lar lymphoma， occurs mostly in patients >60 years old and is clinically characterized by unilateral painless scrotal swelling； high incidence of bilateral involvement (35%)； frequent spread to the skin， central nervous system (CNS)， lung， and Waldeyer’s ring； and aggressive clinical behavior with poor prognosis， especially in patients with advanced disease 通用删除6(英):<u>\[1-10\]</u>. Testis may be rarely involved by mantle cell lymphoma (MCL)， Burkitt lymphoma (BL)， peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL)， not oth-erwise specified， anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL)， and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma， nasal type (ENKTL).

【112】**B-CELL NEOPLASMS**

【113】**DIFFUSE LARGE B-CELL LYMPHOMA**

【114】**Introduction**

Primary testicular DLBCL has a poor prognosis despite localized presentation and doxorubicin-based chemotherapy通用删除6(英):<u>\[2，3，5，7，11\]</u>. Extratesticular dissemination (often to the CNS) is common. Adding the rituximab to the treatment protocol in|删除0换行|the last decade did not improve significantly disease-free sur-vival in patients with testicular DLBCL (as opposed to nodal disease， where there is a significant improvement in outcome after addition of rituximab). Approximately 50% of patients with testicular DLBCL present with stage II-IV disease 通用删除6(英):<u>\[7\]</u>. Touroutoglou et al. 通用删除6(英):<u>\[2\]</u> reported that the failure-free survival rate at 153 months was 16% for all patients or 32% and 0% for those with International Prognostic Index (IPI) scores ≤l and>l， respectively. The CNS or contralateral testis was involved in all patients who failed to respond to primary therapy and in 50% of those who relapsed from complete remission. In a series reported by Darby et al.， 40% of patients with testicu-lar lymphoma relapsed following a complete response and a median time to relapse was 9 months 通用删除6(英):<u>\[8\]</u>. Only one of these relapses was in the CNS， one in the bone， one in the skin， and two in the contralateral testis. The majority of relapses (58%) occurred in the lymph nodes.

【9】Acute secondary peritonitis is usually due to entry of enteric bacte-ria into the peritoneal cavity from an inflamed appendix， intus-susception， volvulus， rupture of Meckel’s diverticulum， incarcer-ated hernia， peptic ulcer， ulcerative colitis， pseudo-membranous enterocolitis， meconium ileus， necrotizing enterocolitis， etc. Dif-fuse abdominal pain， fever， nausea， and vomiting are the usual presenting complaints.Thee physical findingsincludee rrebound tenderness， abdominal wall rigidity， sluggish or absentbowel sounds， and shock. Eventually， the child may develop progressive toxemia. Leukocytosis vwith predominance of polymorphonuclear cells is characteristic.

【10】This condition， in which there is swelling and inflammation of the mesenteric lymph glands in the ileocecal region in particular， may be clinically indistinguishable from acute appendicitis. Among the causative _agents rank viruses， Yersinia enterocolitica， E. coli， Salmonella and_ _Shigella._

【11】The patient is usually a child above 3 years of age. Following an upper respiratory catarrh， he develops abdominal pain (periumbilical or in the right iliac fossa)， nausea， vomiting， diarrhea or constipation(usually former) and fever. The pain is intermittent. The remissions last a few hours. During remission， the child is comfortable.

【12】The following points may help in differential diagnosis from appendicitis.

【13】1\. Shifting of the point of maximum tenderness on turning the child on his side favors mesenteric adenitis.

【14】2.Temperature tends to be higher in mesenteric adenitis than in appendicitis.

【15】**_3\._ Tenderness is felt nearer the umbilicus and is less well local-ized in mesenteric adenitis than in appendicitis.**

【16】4.Muscle guarding/rigidity over the right iliac fossa in mesen-teric adenitis is not true but only voluntary.

【17】**Differential Diagnosis in Pediatrics**

【18】5\. In a proportion of cases of mesenteric adenitis， it may be possible to palpate the enlarged glands.

【19】6\. Leukocytosis is infrequent in mesenteric adenitis.

【20】In doubtful instances， one may have to resort to laparotomy for establishing the diagnosis.

【21】**Finally， remember that appendicitis and rmesenteric lym-phadenitis may well-coexist.**

【22】Accompanying mild to severe abdominal pain are fever， vomiting， and abdominal tenderness. In advanced cases， paralytic ileus， shock，jaundice， blue discoloration of umbilicus and flanks， disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC)， renal failure and disturbances of potassium and calcium metabolism may complicate the picture.

【23】In suspected cases， diagnosis needs to be established by demon-strating raised serum amylase. Plain X-ray abdomen shows ileus. Barium meal reveals duodenal displacement.

【24】Remember that， though acute pancreatitis may result from sev-eral causes， including viral infection， trauma， drugs (corticosteroids， azathioprine， thiazides)， and malnutrition， its most common cause in pediatric practice remains mumps. Manifestations of acute pan-creatitis follow 3 or 4 days after the swelling of parotid gland(s).

【25】This condition， characterized by telescoping of one of the portions of intestine into a more distal portion resulting in necrosis of the involved segment， is the most frequent cause of acute abdominal pain and intestinal obstruction during the first 2 years of life. Clinical features include episodic pain， vomiting and rectal passage of bloody mucus(current-jelly stools). Fever and prostration are usually present sooner or later. Abdomen is tender and distended. A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable in the upper abdomen in early stages. Rectal examination may show a cervix-like mass and blood on the examining finger. Plain X-ray abdomen may reveal absence of bowel gas in the right lower quadrant and dilated loops of small bowel.

【27】Barium enema may reveal the intussusception as an inverted cap and an obstruction to the progression of barium. In the area of intussusception， there may be a ceiling-spring appearance to the column of barium. _Conservative hydrostatic reductionn gives good results_ 1inan overwhelming majority of the patients. It should be avoided in the presence of strangulation， perforation， or severe toxicity.

【28】Surgical reduction may become necessary in some cases.

【29】**Acute Gastritis**

【30】In acute gastritis， regardless of origin， epigastric pain， tenderness and sensation of pressure and fullness， especially intensifying after food consumption， occur. Nausea， vomiting， belching and lack of appetite are other symptoms.

【31】**Viral Hepatitis**

【32】Nonspecific pain， localized in the right upper quadrant， may occur in some children at the onset of viral hepatitis. Accompanying features include anorexia， jaundice， tender hepatomegaly， and fatty food intol-erance. If jaundice is yet to make its appearance but diagnosis of hepatitis is suspected， you must test urine for bile salts and pigments followed by other liver function test， if necessary.

【33】**Liver Abscess**

【34】Besides pain in the right hypochondrium (often referred to the right shoulder)， the patient is febrile. The liver is enlarged and tender.

【35】Screening shows raised and immobile diaphragm. Demonstration of E. histolytica in stool and aspiration of characteristic anchovy\*sauce (chocolate colored) pus from liver swelling establishes the diagnosis of amebic liver abscess.

【36】**Subphrenic Abscess**

【37】Subphrenic abscess of whatsoever origin (usually it is bursting of a liver abscess， appendicitis， colitis) causes pain
