【56】**Posterior dislocation of the shoulder： Posterior dislo-cations are rare but arc characteristic in patients with seizures， electrical injury， and， occasionally， blunt injury to the anterior aspect of the shoulder. In virtually all cases of posterior dislocation， the humeral head and glenoid remain in the same transverse plane， unlike antcrior dislocation， where the humeral head displaces inferomedially. Some posterior dislocations give the appearance of a widened glenohumeral joint space， caused by “perching” of the humeral head on the pos terior labrum. As a result， the distance between the humeral head and the anterior labrum is widened、which gives the false impression of a widened joint space. This feature is never seen in anterior dislocation.**

【57】**IPseudodislocation of the shoulder： This term applies to a clinical presentation in which physical findings suggest an abnormal position of the humeral head consistent with a shoulder dislocation. Subsequent radiographs fail to show a dislocation but do demon-strate inferior subluxation of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. Pscudodislocation can be seen in the sctting of brachial plexus injury， chronic shoulder joint instability， hemarthrosis， and， occasionally， pyarthrosis.**

【58】**豪DIAGNOSIS： Posterior dislocation of the shoulder.**

【59】**寺 KEY FACTS**

【60】**_CLINICAL_**

【61】**Less than 3% of all shouldeTr dislocations arc posterior. The characteristic setting for this injury is in a patient after a seizure.**

【62】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【63】**__ “Fixed”internal rotation should immediately raise the possibility of posterior dislocation of the shoulder.**

【64】**__ A“positive” rim sign is present when the distance between the anterior glcnoid rim and the humerus is≤6 mm.**

【65】**A post-traumatic “dcnt”in the anterior aspect of the articular segment is called the “trough sign.”**

【66】**Posterior dislocation remains a challenging diagnosis when the axillary or “Y” views are unavailable. Such would be the case on portable chest radiographs obtained for patients with blunt trauma， electrical injury， or seizure disorders. Under these circumstances， it is important to recognize the clues of posterior dis-location on an anteroposterior vicw alone. The radiol-ogist must recognize fixed internal rotation， widening of the joint space (rim sign)， and loss of the overlap appearance (half moon) of the normal shoulder joint as characteristic findings of postcrior dislocation on a frontal film.**

【67】**A post-traumatic dent in the humeral head (trough sign) is a helpful sign but is not always present. Posterior dislocations can also be seen in conjunction with com-minuted fracture-dislocations of the proximal humerus. In any event， the reader should keep in mind that poste-rior dislocations when missed can easily escape clinical detection and become chronic dislocations. It is not unusual for patients with chronic posterior dislocation to remain undiagnosed for months at a time. The radi-ologist must always have a high index for a“missed”posterior dislocation when reviewing outpatient radi-ographs in patients with chronic shoulder pain.**

【68】**A clinical history of any or all of the following symp-toms--a frozen shoulder， limited range of motion， and old trauma-should motivate the radiologist to obtain a dislocation view (axillary vicw preferred) to exclude the possibility of a chronic posterior dislocation.**

【28】**DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS**

【29】**Popliteal cyst： These cysts tend to be located more posteriorly and not as medially as in this case. The neck of a popliteal cyst typically protrudes through the space between the medial head of the gastrocncmius and the semimembranosus muscles， not through the medial joint capsule as in this case.**

【30】**Ganglion cyst： The signal intensity of the loculated collection is consistent with a fluid-filled/jelly-like vis-cous substance. The presence of an associated meniscal tear makes this diagnosis less likely.**

【31】**Meniscal cyst： A horizontal meniscal tear with an associated cyst is characteristic of this diagnosis.**

【32】**Pes anserinus bursitis： Either or both fluid and cdema are often seen in association with inflammation of the pes anserine， namely， the semitendinosis， sarto-rius， and gracilis muscles.**

【33】**DIAGNOSIS： Meniscal cyst.**

【34】**KEY FACTS**

【35】**_CLINICAL_**

【36】**Meniscal cysts contain jelly-like mucinous or synovial fluid. The neck of the meniscal cyst is often traced to the joint line.**

**Meniscal cysts are thought to occur morc commonly on the lateral side of the knee rather than the medial|删除0换行|side， although Burk et al. found more medial meniscal cysts in their series.**

【38】**__ For ganglion cysts， excision of the lesion is sufficient. However， if a mcniscal cyst is excised in a similar fashion， it will typically recur. As such， the diagnosis of a meniscal cyst in this situation rcquircs treatment of the underlying meniscal abnormality to prevent recurrence.**

【39】**__ It has been suggestcd that cysts located posteriorly to the medial collateral ligament are more apt to pene-trate the capsule and to expand in an unrestricted fash-ion. These cysts may be misdiagnosed as ganglion cysts or popliteal cysts.**

【40】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【42】**On proton density or T1-weighted MRI， the tear of the underlying meniscus is identifed. These tears are typically horizontal， with the defect extending to the meniscocapsular junction rather than to the superior or inferior articular surface，**

【53】**学DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS**

【54】**_Anterior dislocation of the shoulder： Anterior shoul-_ der dislocations characteristically cause anteroinferior displacement of the humeral head relative to the gle-noid. This position of the humeral head is never seen in patients with posterior dislocation. In addition， antcrior dislocation leads to total obscuration of the normal glenohumeral joint space due to overlap of the humeral head and the glenoid.**

【55】删除3:<u>**__**</u>

【56】**Posterior dislocation of the shoulder： Posterior dislo-cations are rare but arc characteristic in patients with seizures， electrical injury， and， occasionally， blunt injury to the anterior aspect of the shoulder. In virtually all cases of posterior dislocation， the humeral head and glenoid remain in the same transverse plane， unlike antcrior dislocation， where the humeral head displaces inferomedially. Some posterior dislocations give the appearance of a widened glenohumeral joint space， caused by “perching” of the humeral head on the pos terior labrum. As a result， the distance between the humeral head and the anterior labrum is widened、which gives the false impression of a widened joint space. This feature is never seen in anterior dislocation.**

【57】**IPseudodislocation of the shoulder： This term applies to a clinical presentation in which physical findings suggest an abnormal position of the humeral head consistent with a shoulder dislocation. Subsequent radiographs fail to show a dislocation but do demon-strate inferior subluxation of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. Pscudodislocation can be seen in the sctting of brachial plexus injury， chronic shoulder joint instability， hemarthrosis， and， occasionally， pyarthrosis.**

【58】**豪DIAGNOSIS： Posterior dislocation of the shoulder.**

【59】**寺 KEY FACTS**

【60】**_CLINICAL_**

【61】**Less than 3% of all shouldeTr dislocations arc posterior. The characteristic setting for this injury is in a patient after a seizure.**

【62】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【63】**__ “Fixed”internal rotation should immediately raise the possibility of posterior dislocation of the shoulder.**

【64】**__ A“positive” rim sign is present when the distance between the anterior glcnoid rim and the humerus is≤6 mm.**

【65】**A post-traumatic “dcnt”in the anterior aspect of the articular segment is called the “trough sign.”**

【66】**Posterior dislocation remains a challenging diagnosis when the axillary or “Y” views are unavailable. Such would be the case on portable chest radiographs obtained for patients with blunt trauma， electrical injury， or seizure disorders. Under these circumstances， it is important to recognize the clues of posterior dis-location on an anteroposterior vicw alone. The radiol-ogist must recognize fixed internal rotation， widening of the joint space (rim sign)， and loss of the overlap appearance (half moon) of the normal shoulder joint as characteristic findings of postcrior dislocation on a frontal film.**

【67】**A post-traumatic dent in the humeral head (trough sign) is a helpful sign but is not always present. Posterior dislocations can also be seen in conjunction with com-minuted fracture-dislocations of the proximal humerus. In any event， the reader should keep in mind that poste-rior dislocations when missed can easily escape clinical detection and become chronic dislocations. It is not unusual for patients with chronic posterior dislocation to remain undiagnosed for months at a time. The radi-ologist must always have a high index for a“missed”posterior dislocation when reviewing outpatient radi-ographs in patients with chronic shoulder pain.**

【68】**A clinical history of any or all of the following symp-toms--a frozen shoulder， limited range of motion， and old trauma-should motivate the radiologist to obtain a dislocation view (axillary vicw preferred) to exclude the possibility of a chronic posterior dislocation.**

【80】**Psoriatic arthritis： This is the favored diagnosis given the predominant involvement of DIP joints， presence of erosions with reactive proliferative bone formation， the preservation of bone mineral density， and findings of pencil-in-cup deformity and telescoping of the fourth digit. 【83】**专KEY FACTS**

【94】**Aggressive ccntral erosions may result in joint space widening.**

【1】**Prevalence of HTV-1-Associated Dementia Complex**

【2】**The prevalence of neuropsychological impairment in seropositive indi-viduals varies as a function of disease stage. HAD is the most severe form of neuropsychological impairmert associated with the infection. HIV encephalopathy ， an earlier term for HAD， is the initial manifestation of AIDS in 2.8% of persons with the disease and has been estimated to have a prevalence of 7.3% in AIDS patients based on cases reported to the CDC . A retrospective chart review conducted in specialized HIV outpa-tient clinics at four New York City hospitals found the prevalence ofHTV encephalopathy to be 4.6% among individuals with AIDS . Using a prospective cohort study (Multicenter Aids Cohort Study-MAGS)， MacArthur et al. (1993) reported that HAD is the ini-tial AIDS indicator illness in 3.3% of patients， a figure that is generally consistent with CDC data. The MACS data revealed that the annual inci-dence of HAD was 7% during the two years following an AIDS diagnosis and estimated that one year following the initial AIDS diagnosis， 7.1%of patients will have dementia. However， with the introduction of triple combination therapy， the annual incidence of HAD has been reported to be 1% . The cumulative incidence of dementia in a cohort of 492 AIDS patients from the MACS (Baltimore/Los Angeles site) was 15% over a seven-year period. Day and colleagues (1992) reported a 28% cumulative incidence rate of dementia over 24 months in a much smaller group (N=32) of symptomatic seropositives and an annual incidence rate of 14%. Without an AIDS diagnosis， the preva-lence of HAD is minimat. During the asymptomatic stage of the disease，1987 CDC Stage II & III， the prevalence of HAD is 0.4% .**

【3】**Prevalence estimates of HAD from cross-cultural studies are consis-tent with prevalence rates obtained in samples fron the United States. Using a neuropsychological test battery developed for the World Health Organization's Neuropsychiatric AIDS Study and validated for cross-cultural use， Maj and colleagues (1994) reported the prevalence of HAD amnong HIV-seropositives to be 4.4% to 6.9% across subjects evalu-ated in five centers (Germany， Brazil， Zaire， Kenya， and Thailand). Chiesi and associates (1996) retrospectively reviewed medical charts and found the prevalence of HAD to be 4.5% at AIDS diagnosis across17 countries in Europe.**

【4】**Prevalence of Minor Cognitive Motor Disorder**

【5】**Minor cognitive motor disorder (MCMD) is a less severe manifestation of HlV-l-associated neuropsychological impairment. Both MCMD and subclinical， mild impairment in cognitive-motor functioning are far more prevalent than HAD . MCMD is most often associated with symptomatic (1993 CDC Stage B) or AIDS indicator conditions (1993 CDC Stage C) . As the disease progresses， the prevalence of cognitive motor impairment increases. For instance， across 13 studies of the neuropsychological effects of HIV l conducted between 1987 and 1995  the medi-an prevalence of cognitive motor impairment was 55% among AJDS patients in comparison to seronegative controls . The rate of neuropsychological impairment in symptomatic seroposi-tives (1993 CDC Category B) is lower； for example， Heaton and col-leagues (1995) reported 44% of study participants were impaired based on clinical ratings.**

**In comparison to symptomatic HIVseropositive individuals， it has been even more difficult to estimate the prevalence of cognitive-motor impairment among asymptoniatic individuals because of the variability in findings across studies . Predictably， methodological issues have been critical to under-standing differences in reported prevalence rates of neuropsychologi-cal impairment in asymptomatic seropositive (ASP) patients. A review of' mostly cross-sectional studies (N = 57) examining mild cognitive-motor impairment in ASP individuals has provided some insight into the nature and degree of impairment in this group. Almost all of the studies (55/57) in the White and colleagues (1995) review used the1987 CDC criteria to classify asymnptomatic HIV (i.e.， CDC Stage II or l). Stage II signifies a fully asymptomatic medical state， and Stage 1I includes persistent generalized lymphadenopathy. This classification revealed a median prevalence rate of 35% of neuropsychological impairinent for ASP persons versus 12% in seronegative (SN) con-trols--almost a three-fold difference. Classitication rates other than median prevalence may yield different findings. Additionally， evalua-tion of the length and comprehensiveness of the neuropsychological assessment revealed that extensive test batteries (more than 14 tests) were approximately three times more likely to find an increased rate of|删除0换行|neuropsychological impairment in ASP patients than studies using fewer than 14 tests. Mode of infection (i.e.， MSM， IVDU， blood trans-fusion，unknown) was also identified as a possible contributor to neu-ropsychological impairment. However， differences in findings were less conclusive due to the methodology and neuropsychological bat-teries used.**

【7】**It is noteworthy that the findings froin the MACS， which studied gay and bisexual men in the most comprehensive assessinent of the neuro-psychological consequerces of HTV-1 infection， revealed that neuropsy-chological deficits are not likely to be seen in ASP individuals when using standard neuropsychological measures . For example， the Miller group (1990) examined769 HIV-seronegative controls with 727 HIV-seropositive ASPs from the MACS study， and found that performance did not differ between groups on any measure. Moreover， only 5.5% of the ASPs in that study showed abnormal performance on individual tests (i.e.， lwo standard deviations below mean for age-and education-matched controls).**

【10】**HIV-1-associated cognitive/motor complex is a term that subsumes minor cognitive motor disorder (MCMD) and HIV-associated dementia complex. Concentration， simple reaction time， executive func-tion， and memory may be impaired in MCMD and are also likely to be affected in HAD. Performance on relatively simple tasks of attention and language are generally preserved until the end stages. Emotionai disturbance (depression) is common in HIV-1 and may be the result of a psychological reactionto the infection； alternatively， behavioral**

【15】**SELECTINGANEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL TEST BATTERY**

【16】**Cultural Status**

【17】**In the section detailing changes in the incidence and prevalence of HIV-1 infection， we emphasized that the demographic profile of indi-viduals with HlV infection in the United States has broadened to include individuals whose primary language is not English and/or whose cultural background is tot American. Sensitivity to demographic factors (i.e.， English language fluency and low education) that might affect individu-als' performance on various neuropsychological measures is particular-ly important. Therefore， in each of the neuropsychological domains listed below， we have included tests in which performance is less likely to be constrained by language and cultural factors.**

【18】**Mental Status**

【19】**Measures of basic cognitive functioning have been found to be limited in their ability to detect early signs of HlV-associated cognitive/motor complex . For instance， measures like the Mini-Mental Status Examination  and the Mattis Dementia Rating Scale  are less sensitive to HAD because they primarily assess symptoms typically found in cortical dementia (i.e.， language impairment， visuospatial deficits) rather than subcortical processes(L.e.， psychomotor speed， working meinory). Among the mental status screening instrumerts， the Mini-Mental Status Examination has been found to be useful only after patients reach the moderate stage of HAD and score below the suggested cutoff score .**

**The HIV Dementia Scale  is a screening instrument designed to assess psychomotor speed， concentration， and memory-areas that are often impaired in HAD. The HDS consists of four subtests： timed written alphabet，recall of four items at five minttes， cube copy time， and antisaceadic errors. The HDS was found to identify HAD with a greater sensitivity， positive predictive value， efficiency， and fikelihood ratio than the MMSE (Power et al.). The emphasis on timed tasks makes the HDS superior to the MMSE when assessing patients suspected of having HAD. While the diagnostic efficiency of the HDS is comparable to the Grooved Pegboard test， it is not dependent on instrumnentation (the pegboard) and is less affected|删除0换行|by peripheral neuropathy. Limitations of the HDS include the lack of information about its utility among individuals who are non-English speaking or are from other cultures. Moreover， the HDS may be less sensitive to detecting mild dementia in highly educated patients.**

【21】**Intelligence**

【22】**Overall intellectual functioning is affected by HIV-1 infection ， partially because a subset of the tests is sen-sitive to psychomotor speed. On four of the five subteses that comprise the Performance IQ. higher scores are partially contingent on speed of completion. Digit Symbol (from the Wcehsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised； WAIS-R) has been found to be the most sensitive of the WAIS-R subtests to the effects of HIV-1 infection . It is expected that deficits on Digit Symbol-Coding (from the WAIS-Hl) will be similar or even more pronounced since the length of this subtest was increased with the updating of the WAIS. With the addition of Symbol Search (WAIS-III) to the Performance subtests， a Processing Speed Index can be calculat-ed based on Symbol Search and Digit Symbol-Coding. The Processing Speed Index provides the ability to assess psychomotor speed relative to overall IQ and thus evaluate whether psychomotor slowing is present. With the changing demographics of the HIV1 epidemic， it is recom-mended that for semi-fluent and non-English speaking individuals， non-verbal measures of overall intellectual functioning be used. The Raven’s Progressive Matrices test is considered a more culture-fair test of intelli-gence than the WAIS-R  and mea-sures reasoning ability. Matrix Reasoning， an addition to the WAIS-II， may be a possible substitute for Raven’s Progressive Matrices as the wo tests are conceptually similar， though the convergent validity of these measures has not been tested.**

**HIV1-infected patients usually perform beter on the verbal subtests of the WAIS-R， which， except for Arithmetic， are not timed. However， it is common for patients to have difficulty on the digits backward portion of the Digit Span subtest because of working memory difficulties. With the WAISIlI， a potentially more sophisticated test of working memory func-tion was introduced---Letier-Number Sequencing. This subtest has been validated as a working memory task in individuals diagnosed with|删除0换行|schizophrenia (Gold， Carpenter， Randolph， Goldberg， & Weinberger1997)， and it is likely to be sensitive to assessing deficits affected in HIV1. While the WAIS-Il allows for the calculation ofa Working Memory Index(based on Digit Span， Arithmetic， and Letter-Number Sequencing)， this Index is composed of an amalgam of tasks. For instance， Digits Forward is not considered to be a measure of working memory and it is unclear whether Arithmetic is actually an index of working memory. Therefore， the Working Memory Index may well be useful as a preliminary screen of working memory function that should be followed up with other tests when impairment or lower-than-expected performance is detected.**

【24】**Language**

【25】**Language functions are rarely affected in HIV-1  unless the patient has a focal CNS OI or a CNS tumor affecting the language areas of the brain. On measures of verbal fluency ， the performance of HIV-1-infected individuals has been variable . Deficient fluency can be due to problems other than language impairment， including frontal lobe impairment and psychomotor siow-ing . Speech may be slow due to psychomotor slowing. Dysarthria (slurring of speech) and hypophonia (decreased volume) rarely occur in HAD. Similarly， because of motor difficulties， penmanship may deteriorate. Finally， HIV-l-infected individuals may complain of reading difficulties； however， these are most frequently due to concentration problems rather than alexia.**

【26】**Visuospatial Functioning**

【27】**The majority of studies have found that visuospatial abilities are largely preserved in HIV-1 infection . On timed tests of visuespatial functioning， it is important to clarify whether the observed score is lower than expected due to psychomotor slowing rather than deficient visuospatial ability. Similarly， for an untimed visuoconstructive task， such as the copy portion of the Rey Osterrieth Complex Figure Test， performance may be compromised as the resuit of poor planning and organization rather than impaired visuospatial ability.**

【28】**Attention/Concentration**

【29】**There are several component processes in attention including basic， sustained， and divided attention. Not all of these processes are affected in HIV1 infection， and assessment of attention should be targeted to specific areas. For instance， basic attention is not likely to be affected in HIV-1-infection， unless a delirium (acute confusional state) is present. Several studies have shown that HIV-1-infected individuals perform within normal limits on Digits Forward from the WAIS-R . Even in the early phases of HAD， basic attention is intact . Sustained atten-tion is another domain in which deficits are frequently reported by examinees. Interestingly， to our knowledge， these reports have not been validated in the research literature，possibly because sustained attention measures are not consistently included in study batteries. At least one study found thar HTVseropositive individuals tend to perform within normal limits . Vigilance tasks from contintous per formance tests are recommended for identifying sustained attention deficits. Because no one particular sustained attention task has been val-idated in this population， we do not recommend a specific test for the assessment of individuals with HIV-1 infection.**

【30】**Divided attention is the component of attention most likely to be affected in HIV-1 . Divided attention can be assessed by the Auditory Consonant Trigramns (ACT) Test and the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task(PASAT). These instruments require examinees to hold information in working memory while concurrently performing another task. A few studies have reported impairment on the PASAT among HIV-1-infected persons .**

【31】**Memory**

【32】**Memory impairment is common in HlV1 infection and is a significant sign of HIV-associated cognitive/motor complex. The memory deficit in HIV-1 is characterized by deficient retrieval rather than impaired encoding or retention . As a result， memory deficits in HIV-1-seropositive individuals are most likely to be present during free recall trials in which individuals are not pro vided with cues. Unlike individuals diagnosed with a cortical dementia， HIV-l-infected persons typically have intact recognition ability and will usually benefit from semantic cueing (i.e.， reminders that focus the examinee toward the specific category that encompasses the items).**

【33】**Assessment of memory in HIV-infected individuals is critical because of the functional implications of a deficit. Measures of list learning (i.e.， California Verbal Learning Test， Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test) are particularly sensitive to detecting memory difficulties as they require more effortful processing and are less dependent on contextual information than paragraph recall (i.e.， WMS-III： Logical MemoryI&l).**

【34】**While these traditional list learning tasks have been lested on English-speaking populations， the changing demographics of HIV-1indicate the need to be sensitive to the moderating effects of culture. The WHO/UCLA Auditory Verbal Learning Test， developed for and used in the World Health Organization's multicenter study of HIV infection ， may be more appropriate for Spanish-speaking individuals. The WHO/UCLA Auditory Verbal Learning Test is similar to the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test； however， the items that comprise the WHO/UCLA Auditory Verbal Learning Test were selected to be familiar to a variety of cultures (Mai et al.).**

【35】**Like verbal memory， nonverbal memory is often affected in HIV-1. The research on nonverbal memory impairment has been inconsistent， but generally is affected by HIV-1infection. Discrepancies between verbal and nonverbal memory may indicate a focal process. Assessment of nonverbal memory can be accomplished using the Rey Osterrieth Complex Figure Delayed Recall or visual memory tasks from the WMS-I

【7】**Less common diagnostic considerations**

【8】Less common causes of diarrhea include amebiasis， pinworm， bacterial overgrowth after abdominal surgery，achlorhydria， gastric stasis (in diabetes)， carcinoid syndrome， blind loop syndrome with bacterial overgrowth， inflammatory bowel disease， Crohn’s disease， ulcerative colitis， and radiation colitis.

【9】Antidiarrheal drugs can result in obstipation. With obstipation and fecal impaction (which is more common in elderly patients)， there may be frequent small， loose， and watery bowel movements without much solid stool. Fecal impaction can usually be diagnosed by rectal examination.

【10】Patients with inflammatory bowel disease usually have frequent small stools or diarrhea with the passage of blood， mucus， and occasionally pus. They often have rectal leakage， nocturnal diarrhea， pain， urgency， and early-morning rushes. With the acute form， patients may appear toxic and have malaise， fever， dehydration， and tachycardia. Those with chronic inflammatory bowel disease may have weight loss， anemia， joint pains， and skin lesions (e.g.， erythema nodosum).

【11】Intestinal ischemia (bloody diarrhea from ischemic colitis or severe diarrhea from small-bowel ischemia) should be considered in all patients who have experienced shock or a hypotensive episode.

【12】Malabsorption conditions other than lactose intolerance include adult nontropical celiac sprue (a gluten sensitivity)； intolerance to carbohydrates， cow’s milk， or protein； and loss of absorptive surface due to bowel resection or sprue. Maldigestion results from inadequate bile acid concentration or pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.

Pancreatic islet cell tumors and colorectal carcinoma may present initially with diarrhea. Colorectal cancer is more common in middle-aged than elderly patients and may manifest as any change in bowel habits， most often diarrhea alternating with constipation. Diarrhea may be the only presenting symptom， particularly if the lesion is in|删除换行|the cecum or ascending colon.

【14】**Chronic diarrhea in children**

【15】The specific time that must elapse for diarrhea to be considered chronic is a matter of controversy. It is generally believed that diarrhea in a child must persist for 1 or more months to be considered chronic. In addition， the child must have either lost weight or failed to gain weight during that period for the situation to be considered clinically significant.

【16】The physician must have a concept of normal stool patterns in children. Breast-fed infants younger than 4 months pass two to four stools daily that are yellow to golden， soft， and have a pH near 5.0； formula-fed infants younger than 4 months have two or three stools daily that are firm and have a pH around 7.0. From ages 4 to 12months， most children pass one to three stools per day. These stools are darker yellow and firmer. After age 1， children's stools are formed and resemble adult stools in odor and color.

【17】One approach to the differential diagnosis of chronic diarrhea in children is to classify them by the type of stool： watery stools， fatty stools， or bloody stools. Watery stools are most often seen in the following situations：

【18】·Persistent postenteritis diarrhea (with or without secondary carbohydrate intolerance).

【19】_·Intestinal infections from viruses， bacteria (Shigella， Salmonella， E. coli，_ Yersinia)， and parasites (particularly Giardia).

【20】_·Disaccharidase deficiency； a lactose deficiency secondary to acute_ gastroenteritis is much more common than the primary lactase deficiency. A sucrase-isomaltase deficiency is rare.

【21】Allergic gastroenteropathies， in which the child is allergic to cow's milk protein or soy protein， may also cause watery diarrhea in infants and children. Other much less common causes are Hirschsprung's disease， short-bowel syndrome， primary immune defects， and diarrhea associated with endocrine disorders.

Fatty stools suggest cystic fibrosis， pancreatic insufficiency， celiac disease， or allergic gastroenteropathy. Rarely， drugs such as neomycin|删除换行|may induce steatorrhea.

【23】Chronic bloody diarrhea suggests Shigella or Salmonella infection， _dysentery， inflammatory bowel disease (including ulcerative colitis and_ Crohn's disease)， amebic dysentery， or (less often) antibiotic-induced pseudomembranous colitis.

【44】**Dizziness/Lightheadedness and Vertigo**

【45】Dizziness is a common reason why patients older than 75 years visit their doctors and is associated with an increased risk of falling in the elderly. It is estimated that 14 of people over 65 and 12 of people over85 experience some form of "dizziness."However， most patients who complain of dizziness do not have an ear problem. A careful history is particularly important for these patients. The physician must first determine whether the patient has true vertigo or dizziness/lightheadedness .

【46】参考段删除-1:<u>通用删除16(英):<u>FIGURE 11.1 Algorithm for the initial evaluation of a patient with dizziness. (From Post RE， Dickerson LM. Dizziness： a diagnostic approach. Am Fam Physician.2010；82(4)：361-369.)</u></u>

【47】True vertigo is a hallucination of movement. Objective vertigo is the illusion that one's surroundings are moving. Subjective vertigo is the feeling that， with eyes closed， one's body or head is moving or turning in space.

【48】In contrast， lightheadedness， dizziness， and giddiness represent a sensation of being about to faint (near-syncope)； this is not accompanied by true syncope or a feeling of rotation or movement.

【49】Some patients describe lightheadedness as a lack of strength or a generalized weakness and may feel that they will pass out if they do not lie down； this symptom usually improves rapidly with recumbency. Lightheadedness， dizziness， and near-syncope must be differentiated from true syncope (not discussed in this chapter)， which has more serious implications， especially in elderly patients.

【50】**True vertigo Nature of Patient**

【51】Most vertiginous episodes in children are benign and self-limiting， except those associated with a seizure disorder. Vertigo is seldom the initial symptom of a seizure； when it is， it may be followed by transitory unconsciousness or amnesia of the event. Although true vertigo is uncommon in children， they may complain of vertigo after _an upper respiratory tract infection or an acute viral infection in which_ hearing was also disturbed. The most common causes of vertigo in _children are migraine or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)，_ often referred to as benign positional vertigo. Vertigo may be secondary to acute viral laburinthitis. Children with serous otitis media do not usually complain of dizziness or vertigo but may have nondescript balance disturbances. Vertigo or headaches may develop in children several weeks after a head injury. When paroxysmal vertigo occurs in children with a family history of migraine， it may represent a _vestibular migraine._

【52】In adults， true vertigo is frequently caused by BPPV， Menière’s syndrome (or disease)， and labyrinthitis. Ototoxic and salt-retaining drugs， acoustic neuroma， and brainstem dysfunction are less common causes.

【53】To facilitate diagnosis， vertigo can be separated into central and peripheral causes. Central vertigo is caused by brainstem or cerebellar lesions and is associated with diplopia， dysarthria， dysphagia， paresthesias， headache， and ataxia. Peripheral vertigo is caused by problems of the inner ear or vestibular nerve and can often be diagnosed from the duration of symptoms.

【54】**Nature of Symptoms**

【55】Although the clinical differential diagnosis of vertigo is best made based on associated symptoms， physical findings， and diagnostic studies， vertigo has some distinguishing features.

【56】Peripheral vertigo is usually severe， has a sudden onset， lasts seconds to minutes， is related to position， is fatigable， and has associated auditory symptoms and horizontal nystagmus.

【57】Central vertigo is mild， has a gradual onset， lasts weeks to months， is not related to position， is not fatigable， and has associated neurologic and visual symptoms and vertical nystagmus.

【58】Recurrent attacks are often associated with BPPV and Meniere's syndrome， and labyrinthitis is usually not recurrent. The vertigo associated with otitis media has a gradual onset and may persist after the otitis subsides. If the vertigo has been continuous andprogressive for several weeks or months， a mass lesion should be suspected.

【59】BPPV， Meniere's syndrome， and labyrinthitis have varying durations of symptoms. In positional vertigo， symptoms last from seconds to minutes； in vertebrobasilar insufficiency， symptoms last for minutes； in Meniere's syndrome， symptoms last from minutes to hours； and in toxic labyrinthitis， vestibular neuronitis， or brainstem lesion， symptoms last from days to weeks.

【60】Prior episodes of vertigo may have been correctly diagnosed. However， if the previous physician did not obtain a precise history and perform an appropriate physical examination， prior episodes of vertigo may have been misdiagnosed as "nerves，"“tension，"or“low blood pressure."Lack of physician awareness of BPPV is a common cause of the misdiagnosis of dizziness in elderly people.

【61】**Associated Symptoms**

【62】Tinnitus， ear fullness， and other hearing disturbances are usually present with Meniere's syndrome， rare in labyrinthitis， and absent in BPPV. Nausea and vomiting may be present in all. If vertigo is associated with an acute onset of unilateral weakness， problems with coordination， diplopia， or numbness， the vertigo is caused by brainstem disease， such as vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Patients with such diseases usually have normal hearing but may have other signs of brainstem dysfunction (e.g.， vertical， lateral， or rotatory nystagmus).

【15】Some benign and malignant cutaneous lymphoid infiltrates may exhibit accentuation around hair follicles . This perifollicu-lar pattern may or may not be associated with disruption of follicular architecture and infiltra-tion of the follicular epithelium by lymphocytes(folliculotropism). Sebaceous glands are often diminished. A perifollicular distribution may be the main pattern or may be associated with other histopathologic patterns.

【16】Cutaneous marginal zone B-cell lymphoma frequently demonstrates vertical orientation of the lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate adjacent to hair follicles. This pattern resembles a blue column in the dermis . Plasma cells are generally present at the periphery of the infiltrate， and monotypic expression of immunoglobulin light chain can be detected via immunohistochemistry or in situ hybridization.

【17】Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides is a variant of mycosis fungoides showing tropism for hair follicles. There is prominent infiltration of the follicular epithelium by atypical lymphocytes. Disruption of follicular architecture is also pres-ent and may manifest in several forms： cystic change， follicular destruction with granuloma formation， telogen shift， and basaloid folliculo-lymphoid hyperplasia. Cases of folliculotropic mycosis fungoides with mucin deposition must be distinguished from primary benign follicular mucinosis.

【18】Folliculotropism may also be identified in primary cutaneous aggressive epidermotropic CD8-positive cytotoxicT-cell11lymphoma. Correlation with clinical findings and identification of an immature cytotoxic alpha-betaCD8-positiveT-cell phenotype would help distinguish this aggressive lym-phoma from mycosis fungoides. Another con-dition to consider in this differential would be lymphomatoid papulosis(LyP)， which may occasionally demonstrate a follicular pattern.

【19】A clinical presentation of self-regressing pap-ules and CD30 expression would favor LyP.

【20】Some benign dermatoses may also demon-strate lymphocytic infiltrates with perifollicular accentuation. Some cases of lymphomatoid drug eruption show vertical orientation of the infiltrate adjacent to a hair follicle reminiscent of marginal zone B-cell lymphoma. However， a polytypic pattern is present with kappa and lambda immunoglobulinlight chainstains.

【21】Pseudolymphomatous folliculitis (PF) is a clinicopathologic variant of cutaneous pseudo-lymphoma and generally presents with a soli-tary1lesion showing _a_ dense dermal lymphohistiocyticiinfiltrate with follicular architecture disruption. PF classically lacks T-cell clonality and does not recur after exci-sion. Herpes folliculitis may also show a dense dermal lymphocytic infiltrate. The presence of sebaceous gland necrosis is a clue to the diag-nosis and should elicit searching for herpetic viral cytopathic effect within hair follicles.

【22】Graft-versus-host disease and alopecia areata are also associated with perifollicular lympho-cytic inflammation； however， the density of the infiltrate is quiteemild.Discooiidd lupus erythematosus， lichen planopilaris， and lichen striatus exhibit more prominent lymphocytic interface inflammation (often in both epidermal and perifollicular distribution)， but the degree is unlikely to raise the possibility of lymphoma. In contrast to folliculotropic mycosis fungoides， these entities lack prominent infiltration of the follicular epithelium by atypical lymphocytes. Arthropod bite reactions are also unlikely to raise the possibility of lymphoma； however， the density of the infiltrate may occasionally be denser than usual. Persistent nodular scabies mayoccasionallyexhibit folliculotropism. Careful clinical correlation will prove helpful to prevent misdiagnosis.

【36】**INTRODUCTION**

【37】Dermatologists are not the only physicians who assess and treat patients with skin disorders. The results of the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (1990-1994) showed that US dermatologists saw only 40% of patients with diseases of the skin， hair， or nails. In the primary care setting， 25% of all visits were found to involve skin disorders. Data from both the United States and Canada reveal a continued undersupply

Inflammatory skin eruptions (“rashes") represent a heteroge-neous group of disorders with etiologies ranging from drug reactions to infections (viral， bacterial， or fungal) to autoim-mune attacks on the skin. The pathogenesis of many primary inflammatory dermatoses (eg， psoriasis) is unknown. A small subset of inflammatory dermatologic conditions is particu-larly common in clinical practice. For example， cutaneous drug eruptions represent the most frequent reason for inpatient|删除0换行|dermatology consultation as well as the most common form of adverse drug reaction. Common chronic inflammatory skin conditions include psoriasis， atopic dermatitis， stasis dermati-tis， and acne vulgaris.

【51】**GETTING STARTED WITH THE HISTORY**

Due to the unique accessibility of the skin as an organ， the diagnosis of dermatologic diseases is highly depen-dent on the physical examination. However， the history plays a key role in putting the skin findings in context，|删除0换行|understanding the evolution of the disease process， and arriving at the correct diagnosis. The history is espe-cially important when the eruption is in a later stage or not active at the time of the evaluation， or when only|删除1换行|secondary lesions are present (eg， bullae have ruptured and left erosions with “collarettes"of scale， or all lesions are excoriated and crusted).

【34】**A 23-year-old young woman comes to your office with a rash. The rash started as red， round， pruritic bumps on the abdomen approximately 1 week before presentation and has spread. More recently， 1.5-cm round scaly patches and plaques have developed on the trunk and extremities.**

【36】**INTRODUCTION**

【37】Dermatologists are not the only physicians who assess and treat patients with skin disorders. The results of the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (1990-1994) showed that US dermatologists saw only 40% of patients with diseases of the skin， hair， or nails. In the primary care setting， 25% of all visits were found to involve skin disorders. Data from both the United States and Canada reveal a continued undersupply

Inflammatory skin eruptions (“rashes") represent a heteroge-neous group of disorders with etiologies ranging from drug reactions to infections (viral， bacterial， or fungal) to autoim-mune attacks on the skin. The pathogenesis of many primary inflammatory dermatoses (eg， psoriasis) is unknown. A small subset of inflammatory dermatologic conditions is particu-larly common in clinical practice. For example， cutaneous drug eruptions represent the most frequent reason for inpatient|删除0换行|dermatology consultation as well as the most common form of adverse drug reaction. Common chronic inflammatory skin conditions include psoriasis， atopic dermatitis， stasis dermati-tis， and acne vulgaris.

【36】**INTRODUCTION**

【37】Dermatologists are not the only physicians who assess and treat patients with skin disorders. The results of the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (1990-1994) showed that US dermatologists saw only 40% of patients with diseases of the skin， hair， or nails. In the primary care setting， 25% of all visits were found to involve skin disorders. Data from both the United States and Canada reveal a continued undersupply

Inflammatory skin eruptions (“rashes") represent a heteroge-neous group of disorders with etiologies ranging from drug reactions to infections (viral， bacterial， or fungal) to autoim-mune attacks on the skin. The pathogenesis of many primary inflammatory dermatoses (eg， psoriasis) is unknown. A small subset of inflammatory dermatologic conditions is particu-larly common in clinical practice. For example， cutaneous drug eruptions represent the most frequent reason for inpatient|删除0换行|dermatology consultation as well as the most common form of adverse drug reaction. Common chronic inflammatory skin conditions include psoriasis， atopic dermatitis， stasis dermati-tis， and acne vulgaris.

【51】**GETTING STARTED WITH THE HISTORY**

Due to the unique accessibility of the skin as an organ， the diagnosis of dermatologic diseases is highly depen-dent on the physical examination. However， the history plays a key role in putting the skin findings in context，|删除0换行|understanding the evolution of the disease process， and arriving at the correct diagnosis. The history is espe-cially important when the eruption is in a later stage or not active at the time of the evaluation， or when only|删除1换行|secondary lesions are present (eg， bullae have ruptured and left erosions with “collarettes"of scale， or all lesions are excoriated and crusted).

_ThyroidNodules and Cancer in Graves’Disease_ Thyroid nodules are a common clinical problem in the general popula-tion， but the prevalence of palpable thyroid nodules in Graves’disease is increased by more than threefold compared to the general population 通用删除6(英):<u>\[69\]</u>. Whereas the prevalence of palpable thyroid nodule is 3.2-4.7% in iodine-sufficient areas 通用删除6(英):<u>\[70\]</u>， in one large multiinstitution study the prevalence of palpable thy-roid nodules in patients with hyperthyroidism was 15.8%通用删除6(英):<u>\[71\]</u>. Other studies have reported similar results \[68，69，721.On review of multiple studies， the prevalence of cancer in Graves’disease has been reported to range from 0 to 9.8%， while in Graves’disease patients with palpable nodules the prevalence increased， ranging from 5.8% to 45.8%通用删除6(英):<u>\[69\]</u>. 【19】CLINICAL FEATURESHashimoto's thyroiditis mostfrequently affects middle-aged women and is also the mostcommon cause of sporadic goiter in children. Patients may present with hypo-thyroidism，goiter， or both. Widespread use of thyroid function tests have also identified many cases of Hashimoto's thyroidi-tis with subclinical hypothyroidism characterized with posi-tive anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies in the serum associated with highTSHand normal T4 通用删除6(英):<u>\[98\]</u>. The goiter when present is firm and often lobulated， which may be mistaken for a multinodular goiter or carcinoma. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis presenting as goiterous hypothyroidism has been found to be associated with HLA-D3 and HLA-D5通用删除6(英):<u>\[99\]</u>. It may also coexist with other autoimmune diseases including pernicious anemia， diabetes mellitus， Sjogren’s syndrome， chronic hepatitis， adre-nal insufficiency， and Graves’ disease. There appears to be a familial predisposition for the development of Hashimoto’s thy-roiditis； up to 5% first-degree relatives of patients with Hashi-moto's thyroiditis may have positive antithyroid antibodies in their serum 通用删除6(英):<u>\[99，100，101\]</u>. PATHOGENESIS OF HASHIMOTO'S THYROIDITISThepathogene-sis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis is summarized in Fig. 4. Hashi-moto's thyroiditis is a thyroid-specific autoimmune disorder in which both humoral and T-cell-mediated cellular immune mechanisms play a role. The inflammatory process is initiated by the activation of thyroid-specific CD4 orThelper cells 通用删除6(英):<u>\[107\]</u>. The cause of this T helper cell activation is not entirely clear； both viral and bacterial infections have been implicated 通用删除6(英):<u>\[108-110\]</u>， but there are no conclusive data to support this. Another hypothesis implies that thyrocytes express HLA-DR antigen and become antigen-presenting cells， thereby exposing the thy-roid cellular proteins to the CD4 T helper cells， which initiates the formation of autoantibodies against the thyroid autoanti-gens 通用删除6(英):<u>\[111-114\]</u>.Once the Thelper cells are activated， they stim-ulate the B cells to produce antibodies 通用删除6(英):<u>\[115\]</u> against thyroid antigens such as thyroglobulin， thyroid peroxidase， TSHrecep-tor， and thyroid microsomal antigen leading to antibody-medi-|删除0换行|ated thyroid cell injury. In addition to this pathway of thyroid cell injury， an alternative pathway involving cytotoxicT(CD8) cells and apoptosis has been more recently proposed 通用删除6(英):<u>\[116-125\]</u>. It has been shown that a significant population of intra-thyroidal lymphocytes in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis are of CD8phenotype having a cytotoxic/suppressor activity (reviewed in48，126，127). Some recent studies have shown that follicular cells from tissue samples of Hashimoto's thyroiditis exhibit strong staining for the death receptor Fas and its ligand FasL， together with a high apoptotic rate as compared normal con-trols 通用删除6(英):<u>\[128，129\]</u>. Bcl-2 inhibits apoptosis； immunohistochem-ical studies have shown a decreased expression of bel-2 in thyroid follicles from Hashimoto's thyroiditis patients com-pared to normal controls and also in patients with Graves’dis-ease. Furthermore， interfollicular lymphocytes exhibit weak staining for FasL and strong staining for bcl-2 通用删除6(英):<u>\[128，130，131\]</u>. These data suggest that， in patients with Hashimoto's thyroidi-tis thyroid follicular cells undergo apoptosis by up-regulation of Fas and FasL and down-regulation of bcl-2， which is inde-pendent of the antibody-mediated thyroid cell injury.

【21】PATHOLOGY OF HASHIMOTO'S THYROIDITISSThe thyroid gland in Hashimoto's thyroiditis is symmetrically enlarged and has a pale pink to yellow， lobulated cut surface . The accen-tuation of the lobulations may make the gland appear nodular on gross examination. Characteristic histologic features of Hashimoto's thyroiditis include atrophy of the thyroid follicles with oncocytic (Hurthle cell) metaplasia of the follicular epi-thelium and abundant lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with lym-phoid follicles including germinal centers. In addition there may be varying degrees of fibrosis and foci of squamous meta-plasia associated within the atrophic follicles . The peri-thyroidallymph nodes are generally enlarged and showevidence of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. The degree of oncocytic metaplasia may vary from focal involvement to diffuse replace-ment of the follicular epithelium. In some cases there may be aggregates of oncocytic cells forming partially encapsulated hyperplastic nodules 通用删除6(英):<u>\[30\]</u>. The oncocytic cells may show nuclear enlargement and cytologic atypia. The nuclei of the follicular cells that are associated with the lymphocyticinfiltrate may show clearing of the nuclear chromatin and grooves， which may be mistaken for papillary carcinoma 通用删除6(英):<u>\[5，30，132，133\]</u>. The T cells are pre-dominantly activated CD4+ helpercells with evidence of HLA-DRII expression 通用删除6(英):<u>\[99，112\]</u>. In addition there are associated CD8+ cytotoxic/suppressor T cells intermixed with T helper cells， B cells， and plasma cells 通用删除6(英):<u>\[99\]</u>. As mentioned earlier， the CD8+ cells are thought to play a role in Fas-FasL-mediated thyroid follicular cell apoptosis and cytotoxicity. The plasma cells show reactivity with immunoglobulin G (IgG)， IgA， and IgM heavy chains and both K and A light chains. _Fibrous Variant_ Thiscomprises approx 10 cases and is seen usually in elderly patients who presentwith markedly enlarged goiter and hypothyroidism 通用删除6(英):<u>\[134，135\]</u>. 【9】**TESTICULAR PAIN**

【10】It is helpful but unnecessary to do an anatomic breakdown in developing this differential diagnosis. The mnemonic MINT brings the most important causes to mind instantly

【11】**M-Malformation suggests hernias， varicocele， and torsion of the testicle.**

【12】**I-Inflammation recalls epididymitisandepididymoorchitis.**

【13】**AV N-Neoplasms of the testicles may be virtually painless， but the mass will give them away. Tuberculosis is also unlikely to cause significant pain.**

【14】**T-Traumatic lesions are common in contact sports， but occasionally a boy will deny a history of trauma.**

【15】Referred pain from renal calculi is a significant cause of testicular pain. Any condition that irritates the T12 nerve root (e.g.， osteoarthritis and herniated disc) and the course of the peripheral portion of this nerve (appendicitis) may cause testicular pain， but these are uncommon causes.

【16】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【17】The approach to the diagnosis of testicular pain involves searching for a mass； if it is present， certain questions must be answered. Does it transilluminate (hydrocele)? Can one get above the swelling (testicular mass)? Is it reduc-ible (hernia)? Does supporting the testicle relieve the pain(orchitis)? Ultrasonography is done to distinguish torsion from orchitis. A search for prostatic hypertrophy or prosta-titis should be made， particularly in older men. Smears of urethral discharge， urinalysis and urine culture， cystoscopy， and an intravenous pyelogram (IVP) may be indicated in selected cases. An exploration for torsion or hernia may be the only way to establish these diagnoses.

【18】**THROMBOCYTOPENIA**

【19】The mnemonic VINDICATE is very useful to develop a list of causes of thrombocytopenia.

【20】V-Vascular disorders should help the recall of dissemi-nated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

【21】I-Inflammation： Infectious diseases that may be associ-ated with thrombocytopenia include malaria， rickettsia， toxic shock syndrome， typhoid fever， cytomegalovirus(CMV)， and septicemia.

【22】N-Neoplasms that may be associated with thrombocy-topenia include leukemia， lymphoma， and myeloma； however， any tumor that may invade the bone marrow can cause thrombocytopenia.

【23】D-Deficiency disorders include vitamin Band folic acid deficiencies.

【24】I-Intoxication. This category will prompt the recall of thrombocytopenia associated with gold salts， alcohol， chemotherapy， chloramphenicol， phenylbutazone， radi-ation， thiazides， sulfonamides， and quinidine.

【25】**C-Congenital. This category promotes the recall of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome， Fanconi anemia， maternal drug ingestion， and congenital viral infections.**

【26】**A-Autoimmune. The most important disorders brought to mind by this category are idiopathic autoimmune thrombocytopenia purpura and collagen diseases.**

【27】T-Trauma. Although trauma does not directly induce thrombocytopenia， this category should help to recall transfusion reactions and DIC.

【28】E-Endocrine. This category prompts the recall of hyper-thyroidism and thyroiditis.

【29】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【30】The laboratory workup will provide the best means of diag-nosing the cause of thrombocytopenia. If there is pancy-topenia， the most likely cause is aplastic anemia or bone marrow invasion. Collagen disorders such as lupus erythe-matosus would paint a similar picture. If only the plate-lets are affected， autoimmune disorders would be more likely the cause. The initial workup should include a CBC， blood smear for morphology， sedimentation rate， serum B ， and folic acid levels， chemistry panel， ANA， serum hap-toglobins， red cell survival， and protein electrophoresis. A hematologist should be consulted.

【31】**Other Useful Tests**

【32】1\. Bone marrow examination (aplastic anemia)

【33】2\. Liver-spleen scan (splenomegaly， disease of the spleen)

【34】3\. CT scan of the abdomen (neoplasm， Hodgkin lym-phoma， splenomeg la， aly) Om

【37】**TINNITUS AND DEAFNESS**

【38】If one dissects the anatomy of the external， middle， and internal ear one can obtain an excellent list of conditions to be considered in the differential diagnosis of tinnitus and deafness .

【39】Beginning in the external canal， impacted cerumen and foreign bodies are occasionally the cause. Next， visu-alizing the drum， one is reminded of otitis media， herpes zoster oticus， myringitis bullosa， and traumatic rupture of the drum. Behind the drum are the auditory ossicles； these little bones should prompt the recall of otosclerosis. The chordae tympani nerve passes behind the drum on its way to the jaw and tongue. This structure should suggest the tinnitus of Costen temporomandibular joint syndrome. The eustachian tube should remind one of the aerotitis connected with flying and the serous otitis connected with blockage of the tube from upper respiratory infections and

Moving deeper to the inner ear， one is reminded of toxic labyrinthitis from salicylates， quinine， streptomycin， gentamycin， and a host of other drugs. Classified here is also the "toxic"labyrinthitis ofuremia， anemia， and leuke-mia. Syphilis， typhoid， and other bacteria may occasionally invade the inner ear， but most infections here are viral. The|删除0换行|chronic granulomatous cholesteatoma should be recalled. In visualizing the labyrinth， one cannot help but recall Meniere disease， a prominent cause of tinnitus and deaf-ness. Severe head injuries may cause tinnitus and traumatic labyrinthitis.

【48】D-Degenerative disorders remind one of the idiopathic symmetric tinnitus and deafness in the aged population(presbycusis) and the dominant progressive nerve deaf-ness diseases considered under the congenital category. Paget disease might also be considered here.

【49】**I-Intoxication： It is uncertain whether drugs and certain poisons such as lead， phosphorus， mercury， and aniline dyes affect the nerve or cochlea more， but it is well to remember them here also.**

【50】C-Congenital disorders that may cause tinnitus and deafness include maternal rubella and all the heredi-tary causes of sensorineural deafness. Hallgren disease， Alstrom syndrome， Refsum disease， and Treacher-Collins syndrome are only a few of these. Some of these disorders are associated with lesions in other organs. For example， Alport syndrome is the combination of heredi-tary deafness and nephritis. The aura of tinnitus in epi-lepsy should be recalled here.

【51】**A-Autoimmune diseases that cause involvement of the acoustic nerve and its tributaries indlude multiple scle-rosis and postinfectious encephalomyelitis.**

【52】T-Traumatic conditions include skull fractures and the post-concussion syndrome. The occupational tinnitus and deaf-ness of continuous noise must also be considered here.

【53】**E-Endocrine diseases include hypothyroidism， acromegaly， and diabetic neuritis.**

【54】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【55】When a patient complains oftinnitus and deafness， a good occupational history is essential. Gradual onset of unilat-eral deafness should be considered an acoustic neuroma until proven otherwise. Look for cafe au lait spots on the skin (Von Recklinghausen disease). The combination of other symptoms and signs is the key to a clinical diagnosis. Thus tinnitus， deafness， and vertigo suggest Meniere dis-ease. Almost total unilateral deafness fsudden in onset in a diabetic) suggests diabetic neuritis. A similar episode can occur in syphilis， but vertigo is also often present. Tinnitus and vertigo following a head injury suggest traumatic myr-ingitis， labyrinthitis， or postconcussion syndrome. If there is total deafness with the tinnitus and vertigo， a basilar skull fracture should be considered. Tinnitus and headache suggest migraine.

【56】Diagnostic studies that should be done in all cases are audiograms， caloric tests， and x-rays of the skull， petrous bones， and mastoids. If an acoustic neuroma is suspected， tomography of the petrous bones， a CT scan or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)， and basilar myelography may be indicated. Syphilis and multiple sclerosis require a spinal tap to assist in diagnosis. Angiography (especially if there is pul-satile tinnitus) and EEGs may be required in selected cases

【72】**TONGUE PAIN**

【73】Examination of the tongue is a time-honored important diagnostic aid， but in my experience， it is unusual for patients to present with pain in the tongue. Nevertheless， there is a plethora of causes. The mnemonic VINDICATE lends itself best to prompting the recall of these causes.

【74】**V-Vascular disorders suggest pernicious and iron defi ciency anemia.**

【75】**I-Inflammation recalls Vincent stomatitis， herpes simplex， tuberculosis， and syphilis. The referred pain from gingi-vitis and abscessed teeth should also be considered here.**

【76】**N-Neoplasms remind one that carcinoma of the tongue often presents with pain.**

【77】**D-Degenerative and deficiency diseases remind one of pellagra and other avitaminoses.**

【78】**I-Intoxication and idiopathic disorders call to mind tobacco， plumbism， mercurialism， and glossopharyn-geal or trigeminal neuralgia.**

【79】**C-Congenital anomalies of the tongue are rare.**

【80】A-Allergic and autoimmune diseases， in contrast， suggest dermatomyositis and angioneurotic edema.

【81】T-Trauma suggests the numerous times we bite our tongues and may prompt a search for epilepsy when a patient presents with syncope.

【82】**E-Endocrine disorders remind one of hypothyroidism.**

【83】**_F_ Approach to the Diagnosis**

【84】The approach to the diagnosis indludes a CBC， sedimen-tation rate， serum B.， and folic acid levels， serum ferritin， serology， tuberculin test， and perhaps biopsy of the lesion. A trial of vitamin therapy may be indicated.

【85】**TONGUE ULCERS**

【86】The mnemonic MINT will help the recall of the important causes of tongue ulcers.

【87】M-Malformation suggests malocclusion， which can cause repetitive trauma to the tongue. Also dental prostheses can promote ulceration.

【88】I-Inflammation provokes the recall of herpes simplex， Vincent stomatitis， herpes zoster， syphilis， and tubercu-losis. This reminds one of chickenpox， smallpox， and pemphigus.

【89】N-Neoplasm suggests leukoplakia and carcinoma of the tongue.

【90】T-Trauma is probably the major cause of ulcerations. Repetitive trauma from a sharp， broken， or carious tooth produces painful ulceration.

【91】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【92】Herpes simplex and herpes zoster can be diagnosed by the Tzanck tests， viral isolation， or serologic tests. A fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test will diag-nose syphilis. A biopsy will be necessary to diagnose carci-noma. It is best to refer these patients to an oral surgeon if the ulcers do not clear up with observation and conven-tional treatment.

【93】**TOOTHACHE**

【94】Toothache is included here not only because dentists might read this book but also because physicians are occasionally called on to manage toothache until a den-tist can be reached. A histologic analysis of the tooth and surrounding structures will supply the differential diagnosis. Most commonly， the pulp may be exposed by dental caries， but then the pain is intermittent. When the pulp is infected (pulpitis) the pain is continuous， and the pulp may subsequently become abscessed. The peri-apical tissue may be inflamed， and an alveolar abscess may ensue. Finally， osteomyelitis of the jaw or maxil-lary bones may occur. The gingiva may be inflamed， and pyorrhea will result. What is often not appreciated by physicians is that the tooth can be sore and inflamed without objective evidence on examination. A common cause of this situation is a filling that is close to or in apposition with the pulp.

【95】**Referred pain is as important here as it is in other struc-tures of the head. Thus， sinusitis， otitis media， and tem-poromandibular joint disease may cause pain in the tooth. Trigeminal neuralgia and other neurologic disorders must occasionally be considered.**

【96】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【97】This is simple. Refer the patient to a dentist. If infection is suspected， an antibiotic may be started if there is a delay in getting an appointment. If the dentist cannot find the cause， referral to a neurologist is appropriate.

【98】Torticollis is relatively infrequent； when seen in the adult it is thought to be "supratentorial." There are， however， organic diseases that actually may be responsible. The best approach to recalling these instantly is anatomic， begin-ning with the muscle and proceeding along the nerve path-ways to the brain and "supratentorium.”

【99】**1\. Muscle： These may be divided into intrinsic and extrinsic lesions.**

【100】A. Intrinsic： Hematomas of the sternocleidomastoid mus-cle follow trauma， but congenital torticollis is thought to be due to injury or hematoma of the muscle at birth. Another intrinsic lesion is cervical fibromyositis. In this condition， the head is usually held in one position.

【101】通用删除16(英):<u>**FIGURE 7 Torticollis.**</u>

【102】**B. Extrinsic： Cervical ribs， scars of the neck， tonsil-litis， dental abscess， or cervical adenitis may cause torticollis.**

【103】2\. Nerve and nerve root： Conditions of the spinal column such as cervical spondylosis， tuberculosis of the cervical vertebrae， dislocation or fracture of the cervical spine， and cord tumors can cause this disorder.

【104】**3\. CNS： Tumors of the brainstem and cerebellum can cause torticollis. Some cases are due to postinfectious enceph-alitis and cerebral palsy. Drugs such as phenothiazines and l-dopa may be the culprits.**

【105】4\. Supratentorium： Spasmodic torticollis would seem to fall into this category. I have seen cases begin while a patient is under the pressure of litigation for an occupa-tional injury， especially if he or she is wearing a cervical collar. Hysteria may also cause torticollis.

【106】**Approach to the Diagnosis**

【107】A radiograph of the cervical spine and a thorough neu-rologic examination are axiomatic before one considers the problem to be psychogenic. A Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) will help to support the diagnosis of psychoneurosis， depression， and even malin-gering. Referral to a psychiatrist may be best if the patient is willing.

【108】**TREMOR AND OTHER INVOLUNTARY MOVEMENTS**

【109】Anatomy can assist one greatly in formulating a differen-tial diagnosis of tremor of hepatic coma， Wilson disease and alcoholism. The thyroid brings to mind the tremor of Graves disease. The kidneys signify the tremor of uremia and electrolyte disturbances. The heart suggests the chorei-form movements of rheumatic fever (Sydenham chorea). Finally， the CNS indicates a host of other causes that can be further differentiated by considering the tracts and nuclei of the brain. The substantia nigra and globus pallidus are the sites of Parkinson disease and other related diseases， especially chlorpromazine toxicity. The putamen is the site of gross cavitation and atrophy in Wilson disease. The red nucleus may be involved in the syndrome of Benedikt， a vascular occlusion of a branch of the basilar artery. The tha-lamic syndrome produces a unilateral tremor in the extremi-ties and is caused by an occlusion of the thalamogeniculate artery. Manganese， carbon monoxide poisoning， cerebral palsy， and general paresis all affect the brain and basal gan-glialeading not only to a tremor but also to an organic brain syndrome in many cases. Huntington chorea produces bizarre choreiform movements； it can be recalled by its asso-ciation primarily with atrophy of the caudate nucleus.

【211】**Vascular Disease of the Spinal Cord**

【212】**A. General considerations**

【213】**1\. Vascular anatomy**

【214】**a. A single artery spinal originates from both vertebral arteries， merges and courses from the foramen mag-num to the filamen terminale in the ventral midline. It supplies the ventral horns and white matter of the lower 2/3 of the spinal cord.**

【215】**b. The sulcal arteries arise in turn such that a small segment of the major artery may supply altemate halves of the cord. If occluded over a long enough segment both sides of the cord will be infarcted. X-RT therapy frequently causes a proliferative endarteritis which may occlude only one sulcal0un artery that causes a consequent Brown-Sequard syndrome. Compression of the ventral cord may infarct both sides of the spinal cord.**

【216】**c. The ventral pattern of vascular supply to the spinal cord is similar to that of the basilar artery with mid-line perforators and short and long circumferential arteries. The lateral circumferential arteries give rise to perforating arteries that supply the corticospinal pathways， the ventral white matter and tips of the anterior horn.**

【217】**d. TThhee sulcal arteries supply the ventral gray.**

【218】**e. A posterior spinal artery arises from each vertebral artery to supply the dorsal 1/3 of the spinal cord. This consists of the dorsal columns and most of the dorsal horn (to Rexed layer V).**

【219】**f. The spinal cord is perfused at a very low pressure90/50 mmHg. Many spinal cord vascular events are obscured by major deficits induced by infarction of the cerebral vasculature at equivalent perfusion Dressures.**

【220】**g. The major watershed infarction of the spinal cord often occurs through the pyramidal tract.**

h. Thyrocervical and costocervical branches of the subclavian artery perfuse the cervical enlargement|删除0换行|i. The thoracic spinal cord is perfused primarily by in-tercostal arteries from the aorta and radicular deep cervical arteries. The watershed of the thoracic cord is usually at T2-T4 or T2-T6.**

【222】**The lumbosacral cord is fed by the great radicu-lar artery of Adamkiewicz. It enters the cord from the left side and originates from the ilioinguinal artery derived from the aorta. It usually is found from T9-T12， but may enter the cord at L2. On ar-teriography it is easily recognized by its hair pin appearance. The sacral cord and cauda equina are nourished by vasovasorum from the hypogastric and obturator arteries whose origin is the aorta. These anatomical considerations of aortic origin are im-portant as younger patients suffer infarction of the cord from various arterial procedures.**

【223】**j. The posterior cord vascular plexus whose origin is the paired posterior spinal arteries from the verte-bral arteries are fed by radicular arteries at each level.**

【224】**k. Segmental arteries that supply paraspinous proc-esses may anastomose with vasovasorum of the nerve roots and are often the source of spinal arteri-ovenous malformations.**

【225】**Venous Drainage of the Spinal Cord**

【226】**A. General considerations：**

【227】**1\. This drainage is most important as compression of the spinal cord by facet and ligament hypertrophy as well as traction (spondylolisthesis) may compromise venous drainage and raise cord pressure. This mechanism has been posited for the common myelopathy associated with severe cervical spondylosis. Once initiated， sur-gical decompression does not reverse any deficits， but may halt neurological deterioration.**

【213】**1\. Vascular anatomy**

【214】**a. A single artery spinal originates from both vertebral arteries， merges and courses from the foramen mag-num to the filamen terminale in the ventral midline. It supplies the ventral horns and white matter of the lower 2/3 of the spinal cord.**

【215】**b. The sulcal arteries arise in turn such that a small segment of the major artery may supply altemate halves of the cord. If occluded over a long enough segment both sides of the cord will be infarcted. X-RT therapy frequently causes a proliferative endarteritis which may occlude only one sulcal0un artery that causes a consequent Brown-Sequard syndrome. Compression of the ventral cord may infarct both sides of the spinal cord.**

【216】**c. The ventral pattern of vascular supply to the spinal cord is similar to that of the basilar artery with mid-line perforators and short and long circumferential arteries. The lateral circumferential arteries give rise to perforating arteries that supply the corticospinal pathways， the ventral white matter and tips of the anterior horn.**

【217】**d. TThhee sulcal arteries supply the ventral gray.**

【220】**g. The major watershed infarction of the spinal cord often occurs through the pyramidal tract.**

h. Thyrocervical and costocervical branches of the subclavian artery perfuse the cervical enlargement|删除0换行|i. The sacral cord and cauda equina are nourished by vasovasorum from the hypogastric and obturator arteries whose origin is the aorta. These anatomical considerations of aortic origin are im-portant as younger patients suffer infarction of the cord from various arterial procedures.**

【223】**j. The posterior cord vascular plexus whose origin is the paired posterior spinal arteries from the verte-bral arteries are fed by radicular arteries at each level.**

【224】**k. Segmental arteries that supply paraspinous proc-esses may anastomose with vasovasorum of the nerve roots and are often the source of spinal arteri-ovenous malformations.**

【211】**Vascular Disease of the Spinal Cord**

【212】**A. General considerations**

【213】**1\. Vascular anatomy**

【214】**a. A single artery spinal originates from both vertebral arteries， merges and courses from the foramen mag-num to the filamen terminale in the ventral midline. It supplies the ventral horns and white matter of the lower 2/3 of the spinal cord.**

【215】**b. The sulcal arteries arise in turn such that a small segment of the major artery may supply altemate halves of the cord. If occluded over a long enough segment both sides of the cord will be infarcted. X-RT therapy frequently causes a proliferative endarteritis which may occlude only one sulcal0un artery that causes a consequent Brown-Sequard syndrome. Compression of the ventral cord may infarct both sides of the spinal cord.**

【216】**c. The ventral pattern of vascular supply to the spinal cord is similar to that of the basilar artery with mid-line perforators and short and long circumferential arteries. The lateral circumferential arteries give rise to perforating arteries that supply the corticospinal pathways， the ventral white matter and tips of the anterior horn.**

【217】**d. TThhee sulcal arteries supply the ventral gray.**

【218】**e. A posterior spinal artery arises from each vertebral artery to supply the dorsal 1/3 of the spinal cord. This consists of the dorsal columns and most of the dorsal horn (to Rexed layer V).**

【219】**f. The spinal cord is perfused at a very low pressure90/50 mmHg. Many spinal cord vascular events are obscured by major deficits induced by infarction of the cerebral vasculature at equivalent perfusion Dressures.**

【220】**g. The major watershed infarction of the spinal cord often occurs through the pyramidal tract.**

h. Thyrocervical and costocervical branches of the subclavian artery perfuse the cervical enlargement|删除0换行|i. The thoracic spinal cord is perfused primarily by in-tercostal arteries from the aorta and radicular deep cervical arteries. The watershed of the thoracic cord is usually at T2-T4 or T2-T6.**

【222】**The lumbosacral cord is fed by the great radicu-lar artery of Adamkiewicz. It enters the cord from the left side and originates from the ilioinguinal artery derived from the aorta. It usually is found from T9-T12， but may enter the cord at L2. On ar-teriography it is easily recognized by its hair pin appearance. The sacral cord and cauda equina are nourished by vasovasorum from the hypogastric and obturator arteries whose origin is the aorta. These anatomical considerations of aortic origin are im-portant as younger patients suffer infarction of the cord from various arterial procedures.**

【223】**j. The posterior cord vascular plexus whose origin is the paired posterior spinal arteries from the verte-bral arteries are fed by radicular arteries at each level.**

【224】**k. Segmental arteries that supply paraspinous proc-esses may anastomose with vasovasorum of the nerve roots and are often the source of spinal arteri-ovenous malformations.**

【226】**A. General considerations：**

This drainage is most important as compression of the spinal cord by facet and ligament hypertrophy as well as traction (spondylolisthesis) may compromise venous drainage and raise cord pressure. This mechanism has been posited for the common myelopathy associated with severe cervical spondylosis. Once initiated， sur-gical decompression does not reverse any deficits， but may halt neurological deterioration.**

【228】**2\. Radicular veins at reach level drain into paravertebral and the intravertebral plexus and ultimately the pelvic veins. Thus severe pelvic thrombophlebitis may give rise to venous infarction. The posterior venous drainage is into a large midline vein.**
